title: Dissolving: what water takes, what oil takes, and where the fizz hides

summary.text: Turmeric stains a plastic box yellow and will not wash out with plain water, yet food colour spreads into water at once. A grown-up who bites a hot chilli gets no help from a sip of water, but a spoon of curd cools the burn. A bottle of soda gushes and goes flat when it is warm, but stays fizzy when it is cold. In this unit your child tests which colours dissolve in water and which dissolve in oil, finds out where the gas in a soda is before the bottle is opened, and sees why salt makes ice colder. Then they follow one rule from kitchen jars to the skin of every living cell: a thing dissolves best in a liquid that is like itself.
summary.art: A kitchen counter with two jars side by side, water on the left with red food colour spread through it and oil on the right with golden turmeric colour in it, and a cold soda bottle with a thread of bubbles rising beside them.

intro.hook: Rub turmeric on a white plastic box and then wash it with plain water. The yellow stays. Now rub a little oil on the stain and wipe. The yellow comes off on the oil. Why does the colour leave in one liquid and not the other?
intro.text: Water dissolves some things and not others. In this unit you find out which liquid dissolves which thing. You test turmeric, chilli and food colour in water and in oil. You open a cold soda and a warm soda and find out where the gas was before the bottle was opened. You make kulfi in a bag, using salt on ice. By the end you can say why a grown-up should reach for curd, not water, after a hot chilli.
intro.art: A white plastic tiffin box with a yellow turmeric stain, a bottle of coconut oil beside it, and a cotton cloth with a yellow smear lifting the stain off.

outcomes: I can explain that water and oil each dissolve different things, and test whether a colour goes into water, into oil or into both.
I can say why turmeric stains plastic and why oil or soap lifts it, using the idea that a thing dissolves best in a liquid that is like itself.
I can explain why chilli heat is eased by curd or milk better than by water.
I can show that gases dissolve in liquids, and that a warm drink holds less gas than a cold one.
I can sort mixtures into solution, suspension and colloid using three tests: look, torch and wait.
I can show that salt makes ice melt and makes the mixture colder, and say how dissolved particles change the freezing of water.
I can explain why almost nothing is completely insoluble, and how rain dissolves limestone into caves.
I can tell how Joseph Priestley first made fizzy water, and what people used to believe about air.

terms.meaning: The thing that dissolves. It is the part that seems to disappear into the liquid.
terms.example: In salt water, the salt is the solute.
terms.art: A glass of salt water with an arrow from a pile of salt labelled solute.

terms.meaning: The liquid that does the dissolving. Water is the solvent in most kitchen solutions.
terms.example: In sugar syrup, the water is the solvent. In turmeric oil, the oil is the solvent.
terms.art: Two jars, one of water and one of oil, each labelled solvent.

terms.meaning: How much of the dissolved thing is in a certain amount of the liquid. More in the same liquid means a higher concentration.
terms.example: A tumbler of sea water holds about nine grams of salt. A tumbler with one pinch of salt has a much lower concentration.
terms.art: Two glasses of the same size, one with many salt dots and one with a few salt dots.

terms.meaning: To add more of the solvent so the dissolved thing is spread thinner. A diluted solution is weaker.
terms.example: Adding water to strong sherbet syrup dilutes it.
terms.art: A spoon of dark pink syrup being stirred into a tall glass of water and turning pale.

terms.meaning: Two or more things put together without changing into something new. You can often get them apart again.
terms.example: Sand and salt mixed in a bowl is a mixture.
terms.art: A steel bowl of mixed white salt and brown sand with a spoon.

terms.meaning: A mixture where bits you can see float in a liquid for a while and then settle to the bottom.
terms.example: Muddy water is a suspension. Leave it still and the mud sinks.
terms.art: A glass of muddy water with soil settling to the bottom over three drawings in time.

terms.meaning: A mixture where bits too small to see float in a liquid and never settle. The liquid looks cloudy, and a torch beam shows up inside it.
terms.example: Milk is a colloid. Tiny drops of fat float in the water.
terms.art: A glass of milk with a torch beam glowing through it from the side.

terms.meaning: A colloid made of tiny drops of one liquid spread through another liquid that they do not dissolve in.
terms.example: Milk is an emulsion of fat drops in water. So is the cloudy water after you shake oil with soap.
terms.art: A zoomed-in circle with small yellow fat drops floating among blue water particles.

terms.meaning: A group of atoms joined together that acts as one tiny piece. A water molecule has two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom.
terms.example: A water molecule is far too small to see. A drop of water holds countless of them.
terms.art: A simple picture of a water molecule with one big red ball and two small white balls.

terms.meaning: A gas that has spread through a liquid as separate molecules, so it makes no bubbles you can see.
terms.example: A sealed bottle of soda has carbon dioxide dissolved in it. The bubbles appear when you open the bottle.
terms.art: A sealed clear bottle of soda with tiny dots spread through the liquid and no bubbles.

terms.meaning: How hard something pushes on each bit of a surface. Squeezed gas pushes hard on its container.
terms.example: A sealed soda bottle has a higher gas pressure inside than the air outside.
terms.art: A sealed bottle with arrows pushing outwards on the walls and cap.

terms.meaning: Able to dissolve in oil or fat but hardly in water.
terms.example: The yellow colour in turmeric and the heat in chilli are fat-soluble.
terms.art: A spoonful of turmeric dissolving in warm oil to make golden oil.

terms.meaning: The temperature at which a liquid turns into a solid. Pure water freezes at 0 degrees Celsius.
terms.example: Sea water freezes at about minus 2 degrees Celsius, a little colder than fresh water.
terms.art: A thermometer with a mark at zero and a small ice cube beside it.

terms.example: The salty water in a jar of lemon pickle is brine.
terms.art: A glass jar of lemon pickle with salty liquid around the pieces.

terms.meaning: A coloured substance that gives colour to a thing. Some pigments dissolve in water and some in oil.
terms.example: Turmeric, beetroot and carrot all hold pigments.
terms.art: Three small bowls of turmeric, beetroot and carrot, each with a colour swatch beside it.

terms.meaning: Able to dissolve in oil. Many oily things dissolve in oil but not in water.
terms.example: Camphor dissolves in coconut oil, which is why hair oils can carry its smell.
terms.art: A camphor tablet dissolving in a small bowl of coconut oil.

explanations.concept: Solute and solvent: who dissolves whom
explanations.definition: A solution has two parts. The solvent is the liquid that does the dissolving, and the solute is the thing that dissolves in it.
explanations.description: In salt water, water is the solvent and salt is the solute. In golden turmeric oil, oil is the solvent and the turmeric colour is the solute. The same thing can be a solute in one liquid and not dissolve at all in another. Sugar dissolves well in water and not at all in oil. Turmeric colour dissolves in oil and hardly in water. So you cannot ask only 'does it dissolve?'. You must ask 'dissolve in what?'. Water is the most common solvent in kitchens and in bodies, but it is not the only one. Nail polish remover is a solvent for nail polish, and petrol is a solvent for grease.
examples: Salt is the solute and water is the solvent in rasam.
Carotene, the orange pigment of carrots, is the solute in the orange ghee of carrot halwa.
Nail polish remover is the solvent that lifts nail polish, which water cannot do.
explanations.art: Three jars: salt in water, turmeric in oil and nail polish in remover, each with the words solute and solvent pointing to the right parts.
explanations.context: This card explains the two parts of every solution, because the rest of the unit asks which solvent takes which solute.

explanations.concept: How strong a solution is: concentration
explanations.definition: Concentration is how much dissolved thing there is in a certain amount of the liquid. More dissolved thing in the same liquid means a stronger solution.
explanations.description: Two glasses can both hold salt water and still taste very different. One teaspoon of salt in a big tumbler tastes only a little salty. One teaspoon in a small cup tastes very salty. The amount of salt is the same, but the salt is more crowded in the small cup. Scientists say the small cup has a higher concentration. They often write it as grams in each litre. Sea water holds about 35 grams of salt in every litre. A tumbler that holds a quarter of a litre therefore holds about nine grams of salt. If you add water, you dilute the solution. The amount of dissolved thing stays the same, but it spreads through more liquid, so each sip has less.
examples: Sea water has about 35 grams of salt in each litre.
Sherbet syrup is a concentrated solution of sugar, and a tall glass of sherbet is a diluted one.
A water purifier with a TDS meter shows how many milligrams of dissolved solids are in each litre of water.
explanations.art: A small cup and a big tumbler each with the same two salt dots, the small cup crowded and the tumbler spread out.
explanations.context: This card explains what 'strong' and 'weak' mean for a solution, because the freezing and soda tests depend on how much is dissolved.

explanations.concept: Three kinds of mixtures: solution, suspension and colloid
explanations.definition: A solution has particles too small to see and never settles. A suspension has bits you can see that settle. A colloid has tiny bits that never settle but scatter light.
explanations.description: Salt water is a solution. It is clear, and a torch beam hardly shows in it. Muddy water is a suspension. It is cloudy, a torch beam shows up in it, and the mud settles if you wait. Milk is a colloid. It is cloudy and a torch beam shows up in it, but the tiny fat drops never settle. So the torch and the clock together sort the three kinds. A beam of light shows inside a colloid because the floating bits are big enough to scatter light. The effect is named the Tyndall effect, after John Tyndall, a scientist who studied it in the 1800s. You see it when sunlight comes through the mist in a forest, or through the smoke of an agarbatti.
examples: Salt water, sugar syrup and rasam strained clear are solutions.
Muddy puddle water and atta stirred in water are suspensions.
Milk, fog, smoke from an agarbatti and jelly are colloids.
explanations.art: Three glasses lit from the side by a torch: clear salt water with no beam, muddy water with a beam and mud at the bottom, and milk with a beam and nothing at the bottom.
explanations.context: This card explains the three kinds of mixtures sorted in the Look, Torch and Wait activity.

explanations.concept: Why water takes salt and sugar but not oil
explanations.definition: A water molecule has a slightly positive end and a slightly negative end. It holds on well to things that also have charged or sticky parts, and not at all to oily things that have none.
explanations.description: Water molecules are bent in shape, with the oxygen atom at one end and the two hydrogen atoms at the other. The oxygen end has a tiny negative charge and the hydrogen ends have a tiny positive charge. Salt is made of charged particles called ions, so water grips each ion and pulls it away from the grain. Sugar molecules have many spots that water can hold on to. Oil molecules have none of these charged or sticky spots, so water holds on to other water molecules instead and pushes the oil out into drops that join up and float. Chemists sum this up as 'like dissolves like'. Charged and sticky things dissolve in water, and oily things dissolve in oil.
examples: Salt and sugar dissolve in water because water can hold on to them.
Coconut oil does not dissolve in water because it has no charged or sticky spots for water to hold.
Camphor and wax dissolve in oil because they are oily too.
explanations.art: A zoomed-in water molecule with a red negative end and white positive ends, gripping a salt ion on one side and a sugar molecule on the other, with an oil molecule floating away.
explanations.context: This card explains the rule 'like dissolves like', which you see at work in the Water or Oil test.

explanations.definition: Fat-soluble things dissolve in oil or fat and hardly in water. Many colours, smells and vitamins are fat-soluble.
explanations.description: The yellow in turmeric, the orange in carrots and the red in chilli powder all dissolve in oil much better than in water. That is why cooks fry spices in oil first, and why carrot halwa turns the ghee orange. It is also why turmeric stains a plastic box. The molecules in plastic are oily, so the turmeric colour sticks to them, and plain water cannot pull it off. Oil can. Vitamins A, D, E and K are fat-soluble too, and vitamins B and C dissolve in water. So a little oil with vegetables helps your body take in the orange pigment carotene, which the body can turn into vitamin A.
examples: Frying turmeric and chilli in oil at the start of a tadka spreads their colour and heat through the dish.
Carrot halwa turns orange because carotene dissolves in the ghee.
A greasy hairband and a turmeric-stained box both clean better with oil or soap than with water.
explanations.art: A white plastic box with a yellow stain, a jar of warm oil with golden colour in it, and an arrow showing colour moving from the box to the oil.
explanations.context: This card explains why turmeric and chilli colours go into oil in the Water or Oil test.

explanations.concept: Why chilli burns and curd helps
explanations.definition: The hot part of a chilli is a fat-soluble chemical called capsaicin. It dissolves in fat and hardly in water, so water cannot wash it off, but milk fat and curd can.
explanations.description: When a grown-up bites a chilli, capsaicin sticks to the nerves in the mouth that sense heat. They send a 'hot' message even though nothing is actually hot. A sip of water spreads the capsaicin around but does not carry it away, because capsaicin does not dissolve in water. Milk, curd and buttermilk have fat in them, and capsaicin dissolves into that fat. Scientists also think a milk protein called casein grabs capsaicin, which may help too. Coconut, rice and bread soak up some as well. This is why Indian meals often end with curd rice, and why a spicy dish often comes with raita.
examples: Curd rice, raita and buttermilk soothe a spicy meal better than water.
Washing chilli-cut fingers with oil or soap works better than water alone.
Rice, bread and coconut also soak up some of the hot chemical.
explanations.art: A grown-up with watering eyes holding a glass of water that is not helping, and a bowl of curd with a spoon beside it, with arrows showing the burn moving into the curd.
explanations.context: This card explains why curd soothes a chilli burn better than water, using the idea that chilli heat dissolves in fat.

explanations.concept: Soap has one end for water and one for oil
explanations.definition: A soap molecule has a head that likes water and a tail that likes oil. It sits between oil and water and lets them spread through each other in tiny drops.
explanations.description: A soap molecule is long, like a tadpole. Its head dissolves in water. Its tail dissolves in oil. When you wash a greasy plate, the tails push into the grease and the heads stick out into the water. Soon the grease is wrapped in tiny balls with the heads facing outwards, and the water can carry the balls away. The grease has not dissolved. It has been broken into very tiny drops that stay spread through the water. That kind of mixture is an emulsion. Milk and mayonnaise are emulsions too, held together by their own natural soap-like molecules.
examples: Dish soap lifts oil from a kadai and rinses off with water.
Milk stays an even white because its fat drops are held apart by molecules with a water end.
Hair shampoo lifts oil from hair in the same way.
explanations.art: A greasy plate with tadpole-shaped soap molecules sticking their tails into a grease drop and their heads into the water.
explanations.context: This card explains how soap lets oil and water mix, which you can see when you shake oil and water in a bottle with a drop of soap.

explanations.definition: A gas can spread through a liquid as separate molecules. More gas dissolves when the liquid is cold and when the gas is squeezed to a higher pressure.
explanations.description: A sealed bottle of soda has carbon dioxide gas squeezed into the water at a pressure several times that of the air outside. Under that pressure, a lot of gas dissolves and no bubbles show. When you open the cap, the pressure drops and the water can no longer keep so much gas, so bubbles stream out. William Henry measured this in 1803. He found that the mass of gas that dissolves is in proportion to the pressure. That means doubling the pressure doubles the gas that dissolves. Warmth works the other way. Warm water holds less gas, because the fast-moving gas molecules escape more easily. A warm soda gushes and goes flat quickly. A cold one stays fizzy. Fish need oxygen dissolved in water. Warm water holds less oxygen, which is why fish in a hot pond can gasp at the surface.
examples: A cold bottle of soda keeps its fizz longer than a warm one.
Goli soda has a glass marble held in the neck by the pressure of the gas inside.
Fish gulp at the surface of a hot, still pond because the warm water holds little oxygen.
explanations.art: Two soda bottles being opened, a cold one with a gentle thread of bubbles and a warm one gushing foam, with dots showing gas leaving the liquid.
explanations.context: This card explains the fizz test, in which a cold soda and a warm soda behave differently.

explanations.concept: Salt makes ice melt, and makes the mixture colder
explanations.definition: Dissolved particles make it harder for water to freeze. So salt water freezes at a temperature below zero, and a mix of ice and salt gets much colder than plain ice.
explanations.description: Ice at zero degrees always has a thin film of liquid water on it. Water molecules leave the ice and join it again at the same speed. When you sprinkle salt, it dissolves in that film. The salt particles get in the way, so fewer water molecules can rejoin the ice, but the ice keeps melting. Melting takes heat, and it takes it from the mixture. So the mixture gets colder. Salty ice can reach about minus 20 degrees Celsius. That is cold enough to freeze milk and sugar into kulfi. Sea water freezes at about minus 2 degrees. In cold countries, salt is spread on roads for the same reason, so that ice melts even when the air is a little below zero.
examples: A kulfi seller packs ice and salt round the pot so that the kulfi freezes.
Sea water stays liquid at zero degrees, when a freshwater lake has already frozen.
Salt on an icy road melts the ice, unless the road is so cold that even the salty water freezes.
explanations.art: A pot of kulfi mixture sitting in a matka packed with ice and salt, with a thermometer in the ice reading far below zero.
explanations.context: This card explains why salt on ice makes kulfi freeze, which you test in the Kulfi in a Bag experiment.

explanations.concept: Cell skins: oil and water kept apart
explanations.definition: Every living cell is wrapped in a thin skin made of fat-like molecules with a water-loving head and an oil-loving tail. The skin forms by itself because the tails hide from water.
explanations.description: There is water inside you and water outside you. Each cell needs a skin that keeps the inside of the cell different from the outside. The skin is made of molecules like soap, with a head that likes water and a tail that likes oil. In water they line up in a double layer, with the heads facing the water on both sides and the tails hidden in the middle. Nobody has to build this double layer. It forms by itself. In 1925, two scientists in Leiden, Evert Gorter and Francois Grendel, took the fats out of red blood cells and spread them out. They found that there was just enough to cover each cell twice. That was the first sign that a cell is wrapped in a double layer. So the same rule that sends turmeric colour into oil also builds the skin of every living cell.
examples: Soap bubbles and cell skins both form from molecules with a water end and an oil end.
A bacterium in curd, a leaf cell of a tulsi plant and your own cheek cell all have such a skin.
The skin lets some things in and keeps others out.
explanations.art: A zoomed-in cell skin as a double row of tadpole molecules, heads out in the water on both sides and tails together in the middle.
explanations.context: This card links the oil and water rule to living cells, whose skins form by the same rule.

explanations.definition: Everything dissolves a very little in water, if you wait long enough. A thing we call insoluble just dissolves so little that we do not notice.
explanations.description: Chalk looks insoluble, but a tiny amount does dissolve. Even glass and rock dissolve a little. Rainwater carries a bit of carbon dioxide from the air, and that makes it able to dissolve limestone rock very slowly. Over hundreds of thousands of years, flowing rainwater can carve out huge caves. Some of the longest caves in India are in the limestone hills of Meghalaya. Where the dripping water evaporates, it leaves the dissolved limestone behind as stalactites hanging from the roof. So 'insoluble' is a word for 'dissolves too little for us to see in a short time'. Given enough time, water wears down mountains.
examples: Limestone caves in Meghalaya were carved by rainwater dissolving the rock.
Stalactites form as dripping water leaves a little dissolved limestone behind each time.
The white scale inside a kettle is dissolved minerals left behind by evaporating water.
explanations.art: A cross-section of a limestone hill with raindrops sinking through it and a large cave below with stalactites hanging from the roof.
explanations.context: This card is about the idea that even things we call insoluble dissolve a tiny bit, and what that can do over a very long time.

explanations.concept: The sea holds dissolved gas, as soda does
explanations.definition: The ocean dissolves a large share of the carbon dioxide that people release, which slows the warming of the air but changes the sea.
explanations.description: Carbon dioxide gas from the air dissolves into sea water, as it does in soda. Scientists estimate that the ocean has taken in roughly a quarter of the carbon dioxide that people have put into the air. The gas makes the sea water slightly more acidic. This matters for creatures with shells and for coral, which build their bodies from dissolved minerals. At the same time the sea is warming, and warmer water holds less gas. So scientists are measuring how much more carbon dioxide the sea can keep taking in. Nobody knows exactly how this will change over the next hundred years.
examples: Coral reefs off the Lakshadweep islands depend on sea water that holds the right minerals.
A warm ocean holds less dissolved gas than a cold one, just as a warm soda does.
Plankton in the sea take dissolved carbon dioxide and make food from it.
explanations.art: Arrows of carbon dioxide going from the air into the surface of the sea, with a shelled snail and a coral below.
explanations.context: This card applies the soda idea to the whole sea: gases dissolve in water, and more so when it is cold.

agreed.text: A thing dissolves best in a liquid that is like itself. Charged and sticky things dissolve in water, and oily things dissolve in oil.
agreed.evidence: Salt and sugar dissolve in water but not in oil, while turmeric colour and carotene dissolve in oil and hardly in water. Chemists have measured thousands of cases.

agreed.text: How strong a solution is depends on how much is dissolved in how much liquid, which scientists call its concentration.
agreed.evidence: The same teaspoon of salt tastes weak in a big tumbler and strong in a small cup. Dilution makes the amount in each sip smaller.

agreed.text: More gas dissolves in a liquid when the liquid is cold and when the gas is squeezed to a higher pressure.
agreed.evidence: William Henry measured gas in water at different pressures in 1803. A cold soda stays fizzy and a warm soda gushes and goes flat.

agreed.text: Dissolved particles lower the freezing point of water, so salt on ice makes the mixture colder than plain ice.
agreed.evidence: Sea water freezes below zero. An ice and salt mixture can reach about minus 20 degrees Celsius and freeze kulfi.

agreed.text: Almost nothing is completely insoluble. Everything dissolves a very little in water.
agreed.evidence: Rainwater dissolves limestone and carves caves. White scale from kettles is dissolved minerals left behind when the water evaporates.

agreed.text: A mixture can be sorted into solution, suspension or colloid by looking at it, shining a torch through it and waiting.
agreed.evidence: Salt water stays clear, muddy water settles, and milk scatters a torch beam but never settles.

challenging.for: Shake oil and water in a bottle, and the oil soon floats back up as a layer.
challenging.against: A drop of soap lets oil spread through water as tiny drops, the way fat is spread through milk. A very tiny amount of oil does dissolve in water. And oil mixes perfectly with other oil. Oil and water simply hold on to their own kind best.
challenging.context: This card tests a popular saying about oil and water.

challenging.claim: Water is the universal solvent. It can dissolve anything.
challenging.who: A phrase in many school books
challenging.for: Water dissolves more things than any other common liquid, including salt, sugar, many acids and many minerals.
challenging.against: Water does not dissolve oil, wax, plastic or gold in any amount you could see. Petrol, nail polish remover and oil are better solvents for many things. Water is a very good solvent for charged and sticky things, not for everything.
challenging.context: This card tests the claim that water dissolves everything.

challenging.claim: The fizz in soda is air.
challenging.for: The bubbles look like air bubbles.
challenging.against: The gas in soda is carbon dioxide, which is squeezed into the water at the factory. Air does not dissolve much in water. When the cap is opened, the pressure falls and the dissolved carbon dioxide comes out as bubbles.
challenging.context: This card is about what the gas in soda really is.

challenging.claim: Salt melts ice by making heat.
challenging.for: Ice does melt when you sprinkle salt on it.
challenging.against: The mixture of ice and salt gets colder, not warmer, so it cannot be making heat. Melting takes heat, and the ice and salt mixture takes it from its surroundings and from the milk in the bag, which is what freezes the kulfi.
challenging.context: This card is about why salt makes ice melt.

challenging.claim: Warm water holds more of everything, including gases.
challenging.who: A natural guess after learning that warm water dissolves more sugar
challenging.for: Warm water does dissolve more sugar, and more of many solids.
challenging.against: Gases are the opposite. A warm soda holds less gas than a cold one, and warm pond water holds less oxygen than cool water. What warmth does depends on what is dissolving.
challenging.context: This card tests the idea that warm always means more dissolves.

challenging.claim: Milk is a solution, because it looks the same all through.
challenging.for: Milk looks smooth and even, like salt water.
challenging.against: A torch beam shows up inside milk, which means there are tiny floating bits. Under a microscope you can see round drops of fat. Milk is a colloid and an emulsion, not a solution.
challenging.context: This card tests whether milk is a solution.

big_questions.q: In the Water or Oil test, turmeric colour went into the oil and food colour went into the water. Was that because of the liquid, because of the colour, or because of both? How could you tell?
big_questions.hint: A particle cannot choose where to go. Think about a particle that is held more strongly by one liquid than by the other.

big_questions.q: A sealed bottle of soda shows no bubbles, yet it is full of gas. Where is the gas inside the liquid, and what changes when you open the cap?
big_questions.hint: Think about pressure squeezing gas into the water, and what happens when the squeeze is let go.

big_questions.q: Salt makes ice melt, and the mixture gets colder. How can melting make something colder?
big_questions.hint: Think about where the heat for melting must come from.

big_questions.q: If almost nothing is completely insoluble, is 'insoluble' a fact about the thing, or about how long we are willing to wait?
big_questions.hint: Think about chalk in a glass for an hour, and limestone in rain for a hundred thousand years.

big_questions.q: Every cell in your body is wrapped in a skin that works because oil and water stay apart. What would happen to life if oil and water mixed freely?
big_questions.hint: Think about what a skin around a cell has to do.

big_questions.q: The sea has taken in a large share of the carbon dioxide that people release. What do you think happens to the sea as it takes in more?
big_questions.hint: Think about what carbon dioxide does to water in a soda bottle, and what creatures with shells are made of.

big_questions.q: Milk, fog, smoke and jelly all have tiny bits spread through something else without dissolving. Is a true solution the usual case in nature, or the rare one?
big_questions.hint: Think about the things around you that are cloudy, and the things that are perfectly clear.

big_questions.q: A grown-up bites a chilli and feels heat, but nothing is hot. What is the body telling them, and is the message true?
big_questions.hint: Think about what the nerves in the mouth sense, and what capsaicin does to them.

how_we_found_out.story: For a long time, people thought air was one single thing. In the 1750s, Joseph Black, a Scottish doctor and chemist, heated chalky stones and weighed them. They lost weight, because a gas escaped, and the gas was not ordinary air. He called it fixed air. We now call it carbon dioxide. In 1767, Joseph Priestley, an English minister and scientist, lived next to a brewery in Leeds. Beer was fermenting in big vats, and fixed air lay in a heavy layer above them. Priestley set bowls of water above the vats. The water took in the gas and tasted pleasantly sparkling. In 1772 he published a way to push the gas into water in a bottle. In 1803 William Henry measured how much gas dissolves in water at different pressures. He found that more gas dissolves when the pressure is higher.
how_we_found_out.who: Joseph Black, Joseph Priestley and William Henry
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: People thought there was only one kind of air, and that gases could not be held in water. Black showed that chalk gives off a different gas, and Priestley and Henry showed that water can hold it, more when cold and under pressure.

story.title: The Goli Soda That Went Flat
story.note: The story is made up. The science is real: gas dissolves less in warm water than in cold water, and a goli soda bottle is held shut by the pressure of the gas inside. Meera, her aunt and the cart are imagined.
text: It was a May afternoon in Madurai, and the road shimmered with heat. Meera was nine. Every holiday, she helped her aunt, Selvi Athai, at her soda cart near the bus stand.

The cart held a crate of goli soda. Each glass bottle had a round marble stuck in its neck. When Athai pushed the marble down with a wooden opener, the bottle went pssst, and a stream of tiny bubbles rose to the top. Meera loved that sound.
Athai kept the bottles in a steel tub of water with blocks of ice. 'Cold soda is good soda,' she always said.
That Monday, the ice man did not come. By noon the water in the tub was as warm as tea, and the bottles bobbed in it, half under and half above.

A customer asked for a soda. Athai pushed the marble down. The bottle roared, and a fountain of foam shot over her hand and onto the road. The customer was left with half a glass. After two sips, the soda tasted flat and sweet, with no sparkle at all.
'Weak soda,' said the customer, and put the glass down. By evening, three more people had said the same thing.
Athai wiped her hands on her sari. 'Murugan has cheated me,' she said. Murugan was the man who brought the crates every week. 'He has put weak soda in my bottles. I will tell him not to come again.'
'Maybe it is the heat,' said Meera. 'It is the same soda.'
'The same soda cannot be strong one day and weak the next,' said Athai. 'That is what weak means.'
Her cousin Karthik, who was twelve, laughed. 'Heat cannot change soda. It is just sugar and water and gas.'
'Gas,' said Meera slowly. She looked at the foam drying on the road. Before the bottle was opened, there had been no bubbles at all. Where had all that gas been hiding?

That night she asked her aunt for two bottles from the same crate, with the same date stamped on the side. She took one to the neighbour's fridge. The other she left on the cart, in the sun, for an hour.
The next morning she set out two steel tumblers side by side. Karthik, who did not believe a word of it, held the opener.
First the cold bottle. Pssst. A thin silver thread of bubbles rose, calm and steady. Meera counted to sixty, and the bubbles were still coming.
Then the warm bottle. Pssst, WHOOSH. Foam climbed up the tumbler and spilled over the top. Within a minute the foam was gone, and the water lay still and flat.
Karthik stopped laughing. 'Same crate,' said Meera. 'Same maker. Same day. Only one of them was warm.'

She explained it the way she had worked it out. At the factory, gas is squeezed into cold water so hard that it spreads out in pieces too small to see. That squeeze is what pushes the marble up against the neck and keeps the bottle shut. In cold water, the water holds on to the gas well. In warm water, the gas slips out more easily. So a warm bottle is full of gas that is already trying to leave. When you open it, it all rushes out at once, and the soda is left flat.
Athai picked up the flat tumbler and sniffed it. 'So Murugan did not cheat me,' she said. 'The sun did.'

That afternoon Athai walked to the ice factory by the market and bought a block wrapped in a gunny sack. She put the tub in the shade of the cart's umbrella. She told every customer to open the bottle slowly and not to shake it.
On the way home, Karthik asked, 'Where does the gas go when the soda goes flat?'
'Into the air,' said Meera. 'Some goes into you, as a burp.'
Karthik laughed. This time Meera did too.
story.epiphany: For the parent: a gas can dissolve in water, spread out as molecules too small to see. A sealed soda holds gas at a high pressure, which squeezes a lot of it in, and cold water holds more gas than warm water. When the bottle is warm, the water holds less gas and more of it escapes as soon as the pressure drops, so the bottle foams over and goes flat. The soda was not weak. It was warm. The marble stays up because the pressure of the dissolved gas pushes it against the neck of the bottle.
ask: Why were there no bubbles in the bottle before it was opened, though it was full of gas?
Why did the warm bottle foam over and then go flat, while the cold bottle stayed fizzy?
Athai thought Murugan had cheated her. What did Meera do to check, instead of just arguing?
Why did Meera use two bottles from the same crate and not two from different shops?
What did Athai do after Meera's test, and what science was it based on?

roots.context: We have tested which liquid takes which thing, and where gas hides in a soda. Now we ask what that tells us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: In the Water or Oil test, food colour went into the water and turmeric colour went into the oil. Nothing forced them. Each colour went into the liquid that holds it best. So a thing dissolves in what is most like itself.
deep_truth.habit: We say 'oil and water do not mix' as if the two simply refuse each other. But every colour in the Water or Oil test dissolved in one of them. Whether a thing mixes into a liquid depends on how well that liquid holds it.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Water or Oil test, food colour stayed in the water while turmeric and chilli colour moved into the oil. A drop of soap, which has a water end and an oil end, held on to both.

three.who_am_i: Your body takes in vitamins A, D, E and K with fat, and vitamins B and C with water. So your body has watery parts and oily parts at the same time.
three.what_is_life: Every living cell is wrapped in a skin that forms by itself, because oily tails hide from water. Life is built on oil and water staying apart.
three.what_is_this_world: The sea dissolves gas from the air, as a soda does. Rain dissolves rock into caves. Our world is full of things dissolved in each other.

roots.thread: Water holds on to charged and sticky things such as salt and sugar. Oil holds on to oily things such as turmeric colour and carotene. Soap has one end for each, so it sits where oil and water meet. A cell skin, a soap bubble and a drop of milk all form where oil and water meet. Each thing goes to what is most like itself, and new shapes form where the two kinds meet.

teachings.teaching: Uddalaka asked his son Shvetaketu to put a lump of salt in water and come back in the morning. In the morning the salt could not be seen. But when Shvetaketu sipped from the top, the middle and the bottom, each sip was salty. The Upanishad uses this to teach that the finest essence is everywhere, unseen, and says 'tat tvam asi', you are that.
teachings.link: The gas in a sealed soda is like that salt. You cannot see it, but it is spread through every drop, and you find it when the bottle is opened.

teachings.source: Kabir, a poet-saint of north India in the 1400s, in a couplet sung in many collections
teachings.teaching: Kabir says that everyone knows the drop merges into the ocean, but few know that the ocean also merges into the drop.
teachings.link: In the Water or Oil test, the colour spreads into the liquid, and the liquid changes how the colour looks. Each one changes the other, as the drop and the ocean do. A drop of soap in water does the same.

science.text: A substance dissolves best in a liquid whose molecules hold it in a similar way. Charged and sticky things dissolve in water, and oily things in oil.
The amount of a gas that dissolves in a liquid goes up in step with the pressure of the gas, and goes down as the liquid warms.
How much more carbon dioxide the sea can keep taking in as it warms is still being measured.

other_view.view: 'Like dissolves like' is only a rule of thumb, and it has many exceptions. The real reason a substance dissolves is about energy and disorder: the mixture has less energy and more disorder than the two parts kept separate. Saying that things go to their own kind is a simple way to describe this, not the reason itself.

practice.title: One drop of colour
practice.say: Fill a clear glass with water and let it go still. Add one drop of food colour. Breathe in slowly, and watch the colour open and spread. Breathe out slowly. Breathe in again, and watch the colour reach every part of the glass. Breathe out. Do this three times, then sit quietly and look at the even colour.
practice.kid: Put one drop of colour in a still glass of water. Breathe in slowly and watch it spread. Breathe out. Do this three times.

ask: In the Water or Oil test, turmeric went into the oil and food colour went into the water. What do you think 'like' means when we say a thing dissolves in what is like itself?
If your skin, your blood and the sea all hold dissolved things, where does 'you' end and the water around you begin?
If almost nothing is totally insoluble, is anything really separate from the water around it?

experiments.title: Water or Oil? Which liquid takes the colour
experiments.context: This is the main investigation of the unit. You put three colours into water and into oil, and find out which liquid each colour dissolves in.
experiments.question: Turmeric, red chilli powder and food colour: does each one go into water, into oil, or into both?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Which liquid will take the yellow of turmeric? The red of chilli? The food colour? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Each jar gets the same amount of liquid and the same amount of colour. Every jar is stirred for the same time, and looked at after the same wait. Only the liquid changes between each pair of jars, so any difference comes from water and oil.

materials.item: six small clear glasses, jars or clear plastic cups, each holding about 100 millilitres
water at room temperature, 9 tablespoons in all (3 for each pair of jars)
cooking oil (groundnut, sunflower or coconut oil), 9 tablespoons in all
turmeric powder, half a teaspoon
red chilli powder, half a teaspoon
liquid food colour, 4 drops, or 2 teaspoons of beetroot juice
six clean spoons or ice-cream sticks for stirring, a marker or pen with paper slips for labels, and measuring spoons
a white sheet of paper and a phone torch
a wide bowl of bath-warm water, made by a grown-up, that all six jars can stand in with the water below their rims

experiments.safety: Chilli powder burns the eyes and mouth, so do not touch your face and wash your hands afterwards. Do not taste anything. A grown-up makes the warm water, and it must be only bath-warm, never hot. Turmeric stains clothes and plastic, so wear old clothes and use glass or steel cups you do not mind staining.

schedule.what: Guess, set up six jars, stir, wait, look and write what you see.

experiments.record: Fill in the table, a row for each colour. Draw the six jars at the end with their colours. Then write what you think, what you saw, and why.

cloudy, with red bits that settle
clear oil, with red beads at the bottom

flow.do: Show your child the powders, the water and the oil. Ask for a guess and a reason for each colour. Write the guesses.
flow.say: Here are three colours and two liquids. Where will each colour go, into the water or into the oil? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: There are three colours and two liquids. Where will each colour go? Why do you think so?

ask.q: Why do you think turmeric will go into the oil?
good: Turmeric stains my plate and water does not wash it.
Oil is yellow like turmeric.
Cooks put turmeric in hot oil.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Most children guess that all three go into water, because water is the liquid they know best. Any guess with a reason is a good start. Write the guesses at the top of the table.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Water or Oil test. You guess before you test.

flow.do: 1. Label six jars with a letter and a colour: a water jar and an oil jar for each colour. 2. Pour 3 tablespoons of water into each water jar. 3. Pour 3 tablespoons of oil into each oil jar. 4. Add the same colour to one water jar and one oil jar. Use a quarter of a teaspoon of powder, or 2 drops of food colour.
flow.say: Every jar gets three tablespoons of liquid. Each colour goes in one water jar and one oil jar. Only the liquid changes, so it is a fair test.
flow.kid: Label six jars. Put 3 spoons of water in three jars. Put 3 spoons of oil in the other three. Add one colour to each pair.
flow.parent: Three tablespoons gives a layer deep enough to see colour in. Use a quarter of a teaspoon of powder, no more. Too much powder makes every jar cloudy. Wear old clothes. With 2 to 4 children, each child takes one colour and does their own pair, a water jar and an oil jar. Use the same spoon to measure every jar. One child can take the food colour and beetroot. A child working alone does all six jars, with a parent holding the labels.

check.q: Why does each colour go into one water jar and one oil jar, with the same amount of liquid?
options: So that only the liquid changes
So the jars look neat
So the colours do not mix
check.why: In a fair test, only one thing changes. Here it is water against oil. If one jar had more liquid or more powder, you would not know whether the liquid or the amount made the difference.

flow.context: In this step you set up six jars. Each colour is tested in water and in oil.

flow.do: 1. Stir each jar for thirty seconds with its own stick, counting aloud. 2. Look at every jar at once. 3. Write what you see in the first minute.
flow.say: Stir each jar for thirty seconds. Count out loud. Now look. What do you see in each pair of jars?
flow.kid: Stir each jar for thirty seconds. Count out loud. Look at the colours. Write what you see.
flow.parent: Food colour spreads through water straight away. In oil it stays as red beads and sinks. Turmeric and chilli powder look cloudy in the water and sit in the oil as specks at first. Powders do not dissolve in a few seconds, so the real result comes after the ten-minute wait in warm water.
flow.context: In this step you stir each jar and write down what you see in the first minute.

flow.do: 1. A grown-up stands all six jars in a bowl of bath-warm water, so water and oil are kept equally warm. 2. Wait ten minutes. 3. Stir each jar once more. 4. Hold each jar against the white paper. Shine the torch from the side.
flow.say: Warmth helps colour spread faster. We wait ten minutes. Then we hold each jar against the white paper. Is the liquid clear, or can you see bits floating?
flow.kid: Wait ten minutes. Hold each jar against white paper. Is the colour clear, or are there bits?

ask.q: What is the difference between a colour that has dissolved and a colour that is just floating bits?
good: Dissolved colour is clear all through.
Bits make the water cloudy and they settle.
A torch beam shows up in cloudy water.

flow.parent: Warm oil helps because particles move faster. The oil jars with turmeric and chilli should turn golden or orange-red, with a little powder lying at the bottom. The colour is usually pale in the first ten minutes in cool or damp weather, so if your oil colour is faint, wait ten or twenty more minutes and stir again. If it is still faint, try more powder next time or use ghee that was melted and cooled. In the water jars, turmeric and chilli should look cloudy, with bits that slowly settle, and only a pale colour. If the oil jars look cloudy too, the powder is only floating, which is also a result: write it down.
flow.context: In this step you wait and then look closely. You decide whether each colour has dissolved or is only floating.

flow.do: Fill in the table for each colour. Write what you see in the water jar, what you see in the oil jar, and which took more colour. Give each jar a colour-strength score from 0 (none) to 5 (very strong), judged against the white paper.
flow.say: For each colour, tell me what you see in the water and in the oil. Which liquid took more of the colour?
flow.kid: Fill in the table. For each colour, give each jar a strength score from 0 to 5. Which liquid took more?
flow.parent: Expect turmeric and chilli colour to go mostly into the oil, and food colour to go only into the water. If one of your colours does something different, write exactly what you saw.
flow.context: In this step you write down the results for all three colours.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three things: what they think, what they saw, and why they think it happened.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say three things: what you think, what you saw, and why you think it happened.
flow.parent: These three things are a claim, the evidence and the reasoning. A strong answer: What I think: some colours go into water and some go into oil. What I saw: food colour spread through the water, and turmeric and chilli turned the oil golden and red while the water stayed pale and cloudy. Why: each colour dissolves in the liquid it is most like. Do not explain it yourself before they have answered.

check.q: Turmeric colour is yellow and clear in the oil jar, and pale with floating bits in the water jar. What does this show?
options: Turmeric colour dissolves in oil better than in water
Oil is stronger than water
Water cannot dissolve anything
check.why: The clear yellow oil shows that the colour has dissolved in oil. The floating bits in water show it has not dissolved there. Water can dissolve many things, such as food colour, so it is not weaker. It just holds on to different things than oil does.

flow.context: In this step you say what you think, what you saw, and why.

experiments.title: Fizz and Warmth: does a warm soda hold less gas?
experiments.context: This experiment is about a fizzy drink. You collect the gas that comes out of a cold soda and a warm soda in two balloons, and find out which one let out more.
experiments.question: Two bottles of the same soda, one cold and one warm: which one gives off more gas into a balloon?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Which balloon will grow bigger, the one on the cold soda or the one on the warm soda? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use two bottles of the same drink, the same size, opened the same way. Use two balloons of the same kind, stretched the same way, and swirl each bottle the same number of times. Only the warmth of the soda changes, so any difference comes from warmth.
results_table: What the drink looks like at the end

materials.item: two plastic bottles of soda water or a fizzy drink, 500 millilitres each, same kind and same date, unopened
two balloons of the same kind (a normal party pack is fine), stretched by blowing them up once and letting them go
a piece of string about 50 centimetres long and a ruler
two big bowls: one of ice water (a few handfuls of ice from the fridge freezer) and one of bath-warm water, made by a grown-up; both deep enough to cover most of a bottle
a kitchen sink or a tray, to catch any foam, and a glass for pouring a little out
a watch or phone timer

experiments.safety: A grown-up opens the bottles, slowly, over the sink, because a warm soda can spray. Never shake a bottle before opening it, and keep faces away from the neck. The warm water must be only bath-warm, never hot. A child under six should not blow up balloons by mouth. Throw away the pieces of a burst balloon, because a small child can choke on them. Wear old clothes, as foam may spill.

schedule.what: Chill one bottle and warm one, put a balloon on each, wait, then measure the balloons.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Draw the two bottles with their balloons. Then write what you think, what you saw, and why.
