flow.do: Show your child the two bottles. Ask for a guess and a reason. Write the guess.
flow.say: Here are two bottles of the same soda. One will be cold and one will be warm. Each will blow up a balloon. Which balloon will be bigger? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: There are two sodas, one cold and one warm. Which balloon will grow bigger? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think that balloon will be bigger?
good: Warm things go flat faster.
Heat makes the fizz come out.
Cold keeps the gas in.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Many children think the cold soda will make the bigger balloon, because cold drinks feel fizzier. Write their reason.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Fizz and Warmth test. You guess before you test.

flow.do: 1. Stand one unopened bottle in the bowl of ice water. 2. A grown-up stands the other in the bath-warm water. 3. Leave both for fifteen minutes. 4. Meanwhile, blow up each balloon once and let it go, so it stretches.
flow.say: The cold bottle sits in ice water. The warm bottle sits in bath-warm water. Stretch the balloons while we wait, so they blow up easily.
flow.kid: Put one bottle in ice water and one in warm water. Wait fifteen minutes. Stretch both balloons.
flow.parent: A fifteen-minute wait is enough for the drink to reach the warmth of the water. Do not open the bottles yet. Check that the warm water is only bath-warm. Leave the bottles upright and still.

check.q: Why do both bottles stay unopened while they warm and cool?
options: So no gas escapes before the test starts
So they do not get dirty
So they stay the same size
check.why: If gas escaped before you started, the test would not be fair. Keeping the bottles shut means both start with all their gas inside.

flow.context: In this step you chill one soda, warm the other, and stretch the balloons.

flow.do: 1. A grown-up holds the cold bottle over the sink and loosens the cap slowly, letting the hiss finish. 2. Pour the same small amount (about one glass) from each bottle, so there is room for foam. 3. Quickly stretch a balloon over the neck of the cold bottle. Do the same for the warm bottle with the other balloon. 4. Swirl each bottle gently ten times, in the same way.
flow.say: Open the cold bottle slowly over the sink. Stretch the balloon over the neck at once. Now do the warm bottle the same way. Swirl each bottle ten times, in the same way.
flow.kid: A grown-up opens each bottle slowly. Stretch a balloon on the neck. Swirl each one ten times.
flow.parent: Hold the balloon on the neck with your hand, as the gas pushes it. Open the warm bottle very slowly, as it may foam. Pour out the same amount from each bottle first, so foam does not rush into the balloon. If foam does get in, the balloon still shows the difference. Stand both bottles back in their bowls and leave them for five minutes. If the balloon comes off, put it back quickly, and tie a rubber band round the neck if it keeps slipping. With 2 to 4 children, one holds each balloon, one swirls, one times and one measures. One child alone can do both bottles with a parent. If you have a third bottle left at room temperature, add it as a middle case.
flow.context: In this step you open both bottles and catch the gas in balloons.

flow.do: 1. Wrap the string around the widest part of each balloon. 2. Hold the string flat along the ruler. 3. Write each length in the table. 4. Look at the drink in each bottle.
flow.say: Wrap the string around the middle of the balloon. Mark where it meets. Lay it along the ruler. Which balloon is bigger? What does the drink in each bottle look like now?
flow.kid: Wrap the string round each balloon. Measure it on the ruler. Write the numbers.
flow.parent: Expect the warm bottle's balloon to be clearly bigger, and the drink inside to look flatter. The cold bottle's balloon is smaller, and the drink still has bubbles. Your numbers will be different from the example, and a balloon can be small or large depending on how stretchy it is, so compare the two balloons only with each other. If the two balloons are the same size, swirl the warm bottle ten more times and measure again. If both are tiny, the soda was flat before you began, so try a fresh bottle.
flow.context: In this step you measure the balloons and look at each drink.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three things: what they think, what they saw, and why they think it happened.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say three things: what you think, what you saw, and why you think it happened.
flow.parent: A strong answer: What I think: a warm soda holds less gas than a cold soda. What I saw: the warm bottle's balloon went much bigger, and its drink went flat. Why: the gas was dissolved in both drinks, and in the warm drink it escaped more. Do not explain it yourself before they have answered.

check.q: The balloon on the warm soda grew bigger than the balloon on the cold soda. What does this show?
options: Warm soda lets out more gas than cold soda
Warm soda has more gas inside it to begin with
The warm balloon was a bigger balloon
check.why: Both bottles started with the same amount of gas. The warm drink could not hold on to as much, so more of it escaped into the balloon. The balloons were the same kind and stretched the same, so the balloon cannot explain it.

flow.context: In this step you say what you think, what you saw, and why.

experiments.title: Kulfi in a Bag: does salt make ice colder?
experiments.context: This experiment is about ice and salt. You try to freeze sweet milk in two bags, one packed in plain ice and one packed in ice with salt.
experiments.question: Plain ice and ice with salt: which one can freeze a bag of sweet milk in ten minutes?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Will the milk freeze in the bag with plain ice? In the bag with ice and salt? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Both bags get the same amount of milk, the same amount of ice, and the same shaking for the same time. Only the salt changes, so any difference comes from salt.
results_table: Ice only, or ice with salt
The outside of the big bag

materials.item: two large zip-lock bags and two to four small zip-lock bags
one cup of milk (240 millilitres) mixed with 2 tablespoons of sugar
ice, about 6 cups in all (about 40 cubes). Crushed ice works best; if you have little, buy a block of ice from an ice-cream seller or a shop and break it up in a cloth with a hammer
coarse salt (mota namak) or table salt, 6 level tablespoons (about 100 grams, one small packet)
two clean tea towels or a pair of gloves
two clean spoons and a watch or phone timer
a kitchen or fridge thermometer, if you have one (not needed; skip it if you do not)

experiments.safety: Salted ice gets far below zero and can hurt bare skin, so hold the bags in a tea towel or with gloves, and not for long. Do not let salt water into your eyes or mouth. Rinse the small bag under the tap before opening it. Do not do this test with a child who is allergic to milk, and do not eat the milk if the bag leaked.

schedule.what: Fill two bags with sweet milk, pack one in ice and one in ice with salt, shake for ten minutes, then compare.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Draw what the milk looks like in each bag. Then write what you think, what you saw, and why.

setup.art: A cup of milk and sugar being stirred, then poured half into each of two small zip bags and sealed.
setup.caption: 1. Stir the sugar into the milk. Pour half into each small bag. Seal tightly.

setup.art: Two big zip bags each holding three cups of ice and a small milk bag, with salt being poured into only one.
setup.caption: 2. Put each small bag in a big bag with ice. Add salt to one big bag only.

setup.art: A child holding a big bag wrapped in a tea towel and shaking it, a timer on the table.
setup.caption: 3. Wrap the big bag in a towel and shake it for ten minutes.

setup.art: Two small bags taken out and rinsed, one with runny milk and one with soft, slushy, thick kulfi.
setup.caption: 4. Take out the small bags and compare the milk.

flow.do: Show your child the milk, the ice and the salt. Ask for a guess and a reason. Write the guess.
flow.say: We will try to freeze this sweet milk in two bags. One bag sits in plain ice. The other sits in ice with salt. Which one will freeze? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Plain ice, or ice with salt: which one will freeze the milk? Why do you think so?

ask.q: Why do you think that bag will freeze the milk?
good: Ice is cold, so plain ice should do it.
Salt makes the ice colder.
Kulfi sellers use salt, so it must help.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Many children say both bags will freeze, because ice is cold. Write the guess and the reason.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Kulfi in a Bag test. You guess before you test.

flow.do: 1. Stir 2 tablespoons of sugar into 1 cup of milk. 2. Pour half into each small bag. 3. Press out the air and seal each bag tightly. 4. Put each small bag inside a second small bag, if you have one.
flow.say: Stir the sugar into the milk until it disappears. Pour half into each bag. Press the air out and seal it tightly, so no salt water can get in.
flow.kid: Stir sugar into milk. Pour half into each bag. Seal each bag tightly.
flow.parent: A tight seal matters, as salt water leaking in would spoil the milk. A second bag over each small bag is a good extra layer. The sugar dissolves easily in cold milk.
flow.context: In this step you make the sweet milk and seal it into two small bags.

flow.do: 1. Put 3 cups of ice in each big bag, with 2 tablespoons of cold water in each. 2. Put a small milk bag into each big bag, among the ice. 3. Add 6 level tablespoons of salt to one big bag only. 4. Seal both big bags. 5. Label the salty one.
flow.say: One big bag gets ice only. The other gets ice and salt. Everything else is the same. Label the salty bag so we know which is which.
flow.kid: Put ice in both big bags. Add salt to one bag only. Seal both. Label the salty one.
flow.parent: Both bags get the same amount of ice and water, so the salt is the only difference. Coarse salt works best, but table salt is fine. In hot weather the ice melts quickly, so keep the ice in the freezer until the last minute.

check.q: Why does only one big bag get salt?
options: So that salt is the only thing that changes
Because salt is expensive
So one bag can be saltier to eat
check.why: In a fair test, one thing changes. If both bags had salt, there would be nothing to compare. The plain ice bag is the one you compare with. Scientists call it the control.

flow.context: In this step you pack ice round the milk. Only one bag gets salt.

flow.do: 1. Wrap each big bag in a tea towel. 2. Shake and knead each bag for ten minutes, by the timer. 3. After five minutes, feel the outside of each bag through the towel, and peek at the milk in each. 4. If you have a thermometer, read the ice in each bag.
flow.say: Shake and squeeze both bags for ten minutes. Take turns, and share the job with a grown-up. After five minutes, feel the outside of each bag. What do you notice?
flow.kid: Wrap each bag in a towel. Shake it for ten minutes. Feel the outside. What do you notice?
flow.parent: Take turns, as the bags get too cold to hold for long. With 2 to 4 children, one child shakes each bag and a third keeps the timer, then swap. One child alone shakes one bag while the parent shakes the other. The salty bag usually feels much colder, and may have a frosty or damp coat on the outside. With a thermometer, the plain ice reads about zero, and the salty ice reads many degrees below zero, typically around minus ten, though it varies. Warm days and loose ice slow it all down: if the salty milk is still runny at ten minutes, keep going for up to fifteen.
flow.context: In this step you shake both bags for ten minutes and feel how cold they are.

flow.do: 1. Take out each small bag. 2. Rinse it under the tap so no salt water is on the outside. 3. Open it. 4. Look at the milk and write what it looks like in each bag.
flow.say: Rinse each small bag so the salt water comes off. Open it and look. Is the milk liquid, thick, slushy or firm? Which bag froze?
flow.kid: Take out the small bags. Rinse them. Open them. Look at the milk. Which one froze?
flow.parent: Expect the milk from the salty bag to be thick and slushy, like soft kulfi. The milk from the plain ice bag is usually still liquid, just cold. If the salty bag also did not freeze, shake for five more minutes, or add more ice and salt. A bag that leaked salty water into the milk makes salty milk: throw it away. If you want to taste the kulfi, use a clean spoon, and only if the bag was rinsed well and sealed the whole time.
flow.context: In this step you open the small bags and compare the milk.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three things: what they think, what they saw, and why they think it happened.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say three things: what you think, what you saw, and why you think it happened.
flow.parent: A strong answer: What I think: salt makes ice colder. What I saw: the milk froze in the ice and salt bag and stayed liquid in the plain ice bag, and the salty bag felt colder. Why: the dissolved salt lowers the freezing point of the water, so the melting ice gets colder than zero. Do not explain it yourself before they have answered.

check.q: The milk froze in the bag with ice and salt, but not in the bag with plain ice. What does this show?
options: Ice with salt gets colder than plain ice
Salt is colder than ice before it is added
Salt makes milk freeze by itself
check.why: Plain melting ice stays at zero degrees, which is not cold enough to freeze sweet milk. When salt dissolves in the thin film of water on the ice, the mixture gets colder than zero. Salt itself was not cold, and the milk did not freeze by itself.

flow.context: In this step you say what you think, what you saw, and why.

activities.title: Fizz Watch: where does the fizz come from?
activities.context: This is the first thing to do in the unit. You watch a cold soda being poured and look for where the bubbles begin.

materials.item: one chilled bottle of soda water or a fizzy drink
two clear glasses for each child or pair, and a plate to stand them on
six raisins
a spoon and a pinch of salt

schedule.what: Pour the soda, watch where the bubbles start, drop in raisins, and stir one glass to see how quickly it goes flat.

activities.record: Draw the glass with the bubbles. Mark where the bubbles begin. Write one sentence saying where you think the gas was before you opened the bottle.

setup.art: A child slowly pouring cold soda down the side of a clear glass, with bubbles forming along the glass wall.
setup.caption: 1. Pour the cold soda slowly into a glass. Watch where the bubbles begin.

setup.art: Raisins in a glass of soda, some sinking, some rising with tiny bubbles stuck to them.
setup.caption: 2. Drop in six raisins and watch for five minutes.

setup.art: Two glasses of soda, one being stirred hard with a spoon and foaming, one still.
setup.caption: 3. Stir one glass hard for thirty seconds. Compare the two.

flow.do: 1. Pour the cold soda slowly into one glass. 2. Look closely for the first minute. 3. Ask your child where the bubbles begin and where they go.
flow.say: Pour it slowly and watch. Where do the bubbles begin? Where do they go? Before we opened the bottle, was there any gas in it? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Pour the soda slowly. Watch the bubbles. Where do they start? Where do they go?

ask.q: Where do you think the gas was before the bottle was opened?
good: It was in the soda, but too small to see.
It was squeezed into the water.
It was in the air above the water.

flow.parent: Do not explain yet. Bubbles often begin at tiny scratches and specks on the glass, or on the side where you poured. Write what your child says.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Fizz Watch. You watch a cold soda being poured.

flow.do: 1. Drop six raisins into the glass. 2. Watch for five minutes. 3. Count how many times one chosen raisin reaches the top in the first two minutes. Write the number.
flow.say: Watch the raisins. What do they do? Why do you think they move?
flow.kid: Drop in six raisins. Watch for five minutes. What do they do?
flow.parent: The raisins sink at first. Bubbles collect on their wrinkled skins, and the raisins rise to the top. At the top the bubbles pop, and the raisins sink again. They keep dancing, a few trips a minute at first, then slower as the soda goes flat. If nothing happens, use a fresh, very fizzy soda that was cold and unopened, as flat soda will not work; thin-skinned dry raisins work best.
flow.context: In this step you drop raisins in the soda and watch the bubbles lift them.

flow.do: 1. Pour a second glass of the same soda. 2. Stir one glass hard for thirty seconds with the spoon. 3. Leave the other still. 4. Count the bubble streams rising in each glass for ten seconds, and compare.
flow.say: Stir this glass hard. Leave the other still. Which glass has more bubbles left after a minute? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Stir one glass hard. Leave one still. Which has more bubbles left?
flow.parent: Stirring gives gas many places to leave the liquid. The stirred glass goes flat sooner, so it has fewer bubble streams. If you add a pinch of salt to the still glass, it foams up at once, because the grains give the gas somewhere to start. Do it over a plate or the sink and pour the salt in slowly, as it can foam over. With 2 to 4 children, each child can have a glass and test a different thing: stirring, salt, a raisin, or nothing. Do not drink from a glass that has had salt added, or that has been stirred with a spoon used on the table.

check.q: Before the soda bottle is opened there are no bubbles, yet the soda fizzes when it is poured. Where was the gas?
options: Dissolved in the liquid, in pieces too small to see
In the cap
It was made by the glass
check.why: The gas was spread through the liquid as tiny pieces, held in by the pressure in the sealed bottle. Opening the bottle lowers the pressure, and the gas comes out as bubbles. The cap only keeps the pressure in, and the glass does not make gas.

flow.context: In this step you stir one glass and compare it with the still glass. You see how a glass of soda goes flat.

activities.title: Look, Torch and Wait: three kinds of mixtures
activities.context: In this activity you test four glasses with three tests. You look, you shine a torch, and you wait. Then you sort them into solution, suspension and colloid.

materials.item: four clear glasses
water in each glass, three-quarters full
one teaspoon of salt, one teaspoon of soil or fine mud, one teaspoon of milk
a phone torch or small torch and a dark corner or shaded room
a white sheet of paper and a watch

schedule.what: Make four mixtures. Look at each, shine a torch from the side, wait twenty minutes, then sort them.

activities.record: Draw a table with four rows and three columns: look, torch, wait. Write what you see in each box. Then write which kind each glass is.

setup.art: Four glasses of water on a tray labelled PLAIN, SALT, SOIL and MILK, with a spoon beside each.
setup.caption: 1. Fill four glasses. Add salt, soil or milk to three of them. Leave one plain.

setup.art: A phone torch held to the side of a glass of milk water in a dim room, with a bright line of light inside the glass.
setup.caption: 2. Shine a torch through each glass from the side, in a dim corner.

setup.art: The same four glasses twenty minutes later, with soil settled in one glass and the others unchanged.
setup.caption: 3. Wait twenty minutes. Look again.

flow.do: 1. Fill four glasses with water. 2. Label them PLAIN, SALT, SOIL and MILK. 3. Stir one teaspoon of salt into the SALT glass, one teaspoon of soil into the SOIL glass and one teaspoon of milk into the MILK glass. Leave the PLAIN glass as it is. 4. Ask your child to guess how each will look and behave.
flow.say: Here are four glasses. Which of them do you think will look clear? Which will show a torch beam? Which will settle? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Fill four glasses with water. Stir salt into one, soil into one and milk into one. Guess what each glass will do.

ask.q: Which glass do you think will show the torch beam best?
good: The milk, because it is white.
The soil, because it is dirty.
The salt, because salt is white.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guesses. Write them down. Stir each glass for thirty seconds. With 2 to 4 children, each child makes and stirs one glass. One child alone with a parent makes all four.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Look, Torch and Wait activity. You make four mixtures and guess.

flow.do: 1. Put each glass in front of a white paper. 2. Look at it and write whether it is clear, cloudy or milky.
flow.say: Look at each glass against the white paper. Is it clear or cloudy? Is it the same all through?
flow.kid: Look at each glass against white paper. Clear or cloudy? Write it down.
flow.parent: Salt and plain water look clear. Soil water is brown and cloudy. Milk water looks pale and cloudy, though quite even.
flow.context: In this step you look at each glass and write down what you see.

flow.do: 1. Go to a dim corner. 2. Hold the torch against the side of each glass, pointing across it. 3. Look from the other side. Note whether you can see a beam inside the water.
flow.say: Shine the torch through the side of each glass. Can you see a beam of light inside the water? Which glass shows it best?
flow.kid: Shine a torch through each glass. Is there a bright beam inside? Write it down.
flow.parent: A dim room makes the beam easier to see: draw curtains or use a bathroom with the light off. A phone torch is bright enough. The plain water and salt water show hardly any beam. The soil and milk glasses show a clear line of light. This is the Tyndall effect: floating bits scatter light sideways. If the milk glass shows no beam, add another teaspoon of milk. If the soil glass is too dark to see a beam, use a pinch of soil next time.
flow.context: In this step you shine a torch through each glass from the side.

flow.do: 1. Leave the four glasses still for twenty minutes. 2. Do not stir or move them. 3. Look again. Check the bottom of each glass.
flow.say: Now we wait for twenty minutes. Do not touch the glasses. Then look at the bottom of each glass. What has settled? What has stayed the same?
flow.kid: Wait twenty minutes without touching. Look at the bottom of each glass.
flow.parent: The soil settles to the bottom, leaving the water above clearer, though very fine bits can keep it a little cloudy. The salt and milk glasses look the same as before. Milk never settles.
flow.context: In this step you wait and see which glass settles and which does not.

flow.do: Teach the three words: solution, suspension and colloid. Ask your child to sort the glasses into the three kinds using the look, torch and wait tests.
flow.say: A solution is clear and never settles. A suspension is cloudy and settles. A colloid is cloudy and never settles, and a torch shows the beam. Which glass is which?
flow.kid: Sort the glasses. Clear and never settles: solution. Cloudy and settles: suspension. Cloudy and never settles: colloid.

check.q: A glass is cloudy, a torch beam shows inside it, and nothing settles after an hour. What kind of mixture is it?
options: A colloid
A solution
A suspension
check.why: A solution is clear and does not scatter light. A suspension settles. A mixture that is cloudy, shows the beam and does not settle is a colloid, like milk.

flow.context: In this step you name the three kinds and sort your glasses.

activities.safety: Do not shine a torch into anyone's eyes. Soil water is not for drinking, so wash hands after touching it.

activities.title: Thread on Ice: can salt make ice grab a thread?
activities.context: In this activity you lay a thread on an ice cube, add a pinch of salt and try to lift the ice by the thread.

materials.item: a clear glass of very cold water, with a few ice cubes, from the fridge
two big ice cubes straight from the freezer (one for the salt test, one as the no-salt comparison)
a piece of cotton thread or thin string, about 15 centimetres long (a thicker cotton thread or wool works better than very thin thread)
a quarter teaspoon of salt and a watch

schedule.what: Float an ice cube, lay a thread on it, add salt, wait one minute and try to lift the cube.

activities.record: Draw the glass, the ice cube and the thread. Write how long you waited and what happened when you lifted the thread.

setup.art: A clear glass of cold water with a large ice cube floating, and a cotton thread laid across the top of the cube.
setup.caption: 1. Float an ice cube in cold water. Lay the thread across the top.

setup.art: A child sprinkling a pinch of salt along the thread on the ice cube.
setup.caption: 2. Sprinkle a pinch of salt along the thread. Wait one minute.

setup.art: A child lifting the thread and the ice cube coming up with it, hanging from the thread.
setup.caption: 3. Lift the thread slowly. Does the ice come too?

flow.do: 1. Put two ice cubes in a glass of cold water so they float. 2. Lay a thread across the top of each cube. 3. Ask your child whether the thread will lift the ice when you pull it.
flow.say: If you pull this thread up, will the ice come with it? Now, what if we sprinkle salt on it first? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Lay the thread on the ice. Will it lift the ice? What if we add salt?
flow.parent: Do not say what will happen. Most children think the thread will not lift the ice. Try a gentle lift first to show that the thread slides off.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Thread on Ice activity. You guess before you try.

flow.do: 1. Sprinkle a quarter teaspoon of salt along the thread on one cube only. Leave the other cube plain. 2. Count slowly to sixty, or watch the clock for one minute. 3. Lift each thread gently, straight up. Write how long you waited.
flow.say: Sprinkle the salt on the thread. Wait one whole minute. Now lift the thread slowly. What happens to the ice cube?
flow.kid: Sprinkle salt on the thread. Wait one minute. Lift gently. What happens?
flow.parent: It does not work every time. The plain cube is the comparison: its thread should slide off. If the salted ice does not lift, wait another thirty seconds and try again. If it still fails, use a fresh, very cold glass of water and a big cube straight from the freezer, and press the thread down into the wet spot. On a hot or damp day, the cube may melt too fast, so work quickly, and use ice that is frosty from the deep freeze. With 2 to 4 children, each pair gets two cubes and a thread.
flow.context: In this step you add salt to the thread and try to lift the ice.

flow.do: Ask your child to explain what they saw. Then give the explanation.
flow.say: What did the thread do this time? What do you think the salt did? Where did the cold come from?
flow.kid: What did the salt do? Why did the ice stick to the thread?
flow.parent: A strong answer: the salt melted the ice a little, and that made the water around the thread colder than zero. The salty water was then watered down by the melting ice, and the very cold ice around it froze that water again, with the thread stuck inside.

check.q: Why did the thread end up frozen into the ice cube?
options: The salt made a little ice melt and the mixture colder, then the water froze again round the thread
The salt glued the thread to the ice
The thread was colder than the ice
check.why: Salt dissolves in the thin film of water on the ice and makes the ice melt, which takes heat and makes the mixture colder. Then the melting ice waters down the salty water, and the cold ice freezes it again, with the thread inside. Salt is not a glue, and the thread was not colder than the ice.

flow.context: In this step you explain what happened with the thread and the salt.

activities.title: Curd, Water or Oil: what soothes a chilli?
activities.context: In this activity a grown-up who likes spicy food helps you find out whether water or curd soothes the burn of a hot chilli better than doing nothing. The children set the order, keep the time and write down the scores. Children should not eat the chilli.

materials.item: a grown-up who is happy to eat three small pieces of hot green chilli, about 1 centimetre each, or three equal pinches of hot pickle
a small glass of plain water at room temperature
a small bowl of plain full-fat curd (not sweet)
three paper slips marked NOTHING, WATER and CURD, a pen, a sheet of paper and a watch

activities.safety: Only a grown-up eats the chilli, and only a small piece. Do not touch the eyes after cutting or handling chilli. Wash hands afterwards. Do not do this with a grown-up who has stomach trouble, acidity or a milk allergy or lactose problem. Stop and drink milk if it is too hot.

schedule.what: The grown-up eats three equal pieces of chilli, one at a time, with a rest between. After each, they do nothing, sip water or take curd, as the slips say. Record the heat after 30 and 60 seconds each time.

activities.record: Make a table with the rows: nothing, water, curd. Write the heat score from 0 to 5 at 30 seconds and at 60 seconds in each row. Circle the row where the score dropped the most.

setup.art: A grown-up holding a small piece of green chilli beside a glass of water and a bowl of curd, and a child holding a score sheet.
setup.caption: 1. Draw the order from the paper slips. The grown-up eats the first small piece of chilli. Score the heat.

setup.art: The same grown-up sipping water, and the child writing a score.
setup.caption: 2. Do what the slip says: nothing, a sip of water, or a spoon of curd. Score the heat at 30 and 60 seconds.

setup.art: The grown-up taking a spoonful of curd, smiling with relief, and the child writing a score.
setup.caption: 3. Rest until the burn is gone. Repeat with the other two slips.

flow.do: 1. Set out the chilli, water and curd. 2. Explain the 0 to 5 score: 0 is no heat and 5 is very hot. 3. Ask your child to guess what will soothe the chilli best and why. 4. Write NOTHING, WATER and CURD on three slips of paper. Fold the slips and draw them one by one to set the order.
flow.say: A grown-up will eat a small piece of chilli. Then we try water and curd, one at a time. Which do you think will soothe it better? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: A grown-up eats a little chilli. Which soothes it better, water or curd? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think that one will work better?
good: Water washes things away.
Curd is cool and thick.
Milk has fat in it.

flow.parent: Do not say what will happen. Most children guess water. Drawing the order from the slips matters: the first piece may feel hotter than later ones, and a random order keeps one remedy from being unfairly first. NOTHING is the comparison, as the burn fades by itself. If two or more adults are tasting, each can take a different order and you can compare.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Curd, Water or Oil test. You guess before you try.

flow.do: 1. The grown-up eats the first small piece of chilli. 2. After thirty seconds, they score the heat. 3. They do what the first slip says (nothing, one sip of water, or one spoon of curd). 4. They score the heat again 30 seconds later and 60 seconds later. 5. Rest for about eight minutes, until the burn is gone, before the next piece.
flow.say: Score the heat from 0 to 5. Now do what the slip says. Score it again after thirty seconds and after sixty.
flow.kid: Score the heat. Do what the slip says. Score again at 30 and 60 seconds.
flow.parent: Expect the score to change little after water, or even rise as the water spreads the chilli around the mouth. Everyone's mouth is different, so write down what the grown-up says. With 2 to 4 children, one reads the clock, one writes the scores and one asks the score; with one child, you hold the watch and write. If the first piece is too hot, use smaller pieces.
flow.context: In this step the grown-up eats the first piece of chilli and does what the first slip says. The child records the scores.

flow.do: 1. Repeat with the second and third slips, resting between. 2. Compare the three rows: in which row did the heat score drop the most in a minute? 3. Ask whether the score also dropped when the grown-up did nothing.
flow.say: It was the same chilli, the same size of piece and the same waiting each time. Which one brought the burn down most? How much did the burn drop with nothing at all?
flow.kid: Repeat for the other two slips. Which one brought the burn down most?
flow.parent: Waiting until the burn is gone before each new piece matters, or you cannot tell the remedies apart. Expect curd to help more than water, and expect the burn to fade slowly when the grown-up does nothing. One tasting by one person is only a hint, not proof, and the effect can be modest. That is a fine result. Say so, and try it with another adult if you can.

check.q: Why does the test include a piece of chilli where the grown-up does nothing?
options: To see how much the burn fades by itself
To make the test longer
So the grown-up gets a rest
check.why: A chilli burn fades with time. If you only tried water and curd, you could not tell whether they helped or the burn was fading anyway. The 'nothing' piece is the comparison.

flow.context: In this step the grown-up does the same for the other two slips. The child compares the scores.

activities.title: TDS Detective: how much is dissolved in your water?
activities.context: In this activity you use a TDS meter, like the one in many water purifiers, to find out how much is dissolved in different waters. If you do not have a meter, a neighbour, a relative or a water purifier shop may let you borrow theirs.

materials.item: a TDS meter (a small hand-held one, Rs 150 to 400 online or at an aquarium shop; many homes with a water purifier have one, or a neighbour may lend it). No meter: use the evaporation test in step 2
four clean glasses, with tap water, filtered or purifier water, bottled water and tap water with a quarter teaspoon of salt
a fifth glass of tap water with one teaspoon of sugar stirred in
a clean cloth for drying the probe, a pen and paper. For the no-meter test: four clean steel saucers or plates

schedule.what: Measure five glasses of water with a TDS meter and compare the readings.

activities.record: Write the five readings in a table. Draw a bar for each water and mark which has the most dissolved.

setup.art: A small hand-held TDS meter with its metal probe dipping into a clear glass of tap water, the screen showing a number.
setup.caption: 1. Dip the meter's probe into a glass of water. Read the number.

setup.art: Five labelled glasses in a row: tap, filtered, bottled, salty, sugary.
setup.caption: 2. Measure each glass the same way. Rinse and wipe the probe between glasses.

flow.do: 1. Explain that TDS means total dissolved solids, shown as milligrams of dissolved things in each litre. 2. Ask your child to guess which glass will read highest and which lowest. 3. Write the guesses.
flow.say: TDS means the dissolved solids in the water. Which glass do you think reads highest? Which lowest? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Which glass has the most dissolved in it? Which has the least? Why do you think so?

ask.q: Do you think sugar water will read high, like salt water?
good: Yes, because sugar dissolves too.
No, because sugar is different from salt.
I do not know.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guesses. Most children expect sugar water to read as high as salt water.
flow.context: This is the first step of the TDS Detective activity. You guess before you measure.

flow.do: 1. Switch on the meter. 2. Dip the probe into each glass. 3. Wait until the number stops changing. 4. Write it down. 5. Rinse and wipe the probe between glasses. No meter? Put one tablespoon of each water on its own clean steel saucer. Leave them in a sunny, dust-free spot. A few hours later, look at the white rings left behind.
flow.say: Dip the probe into the first glass. Wait for the number to settle. Write it down. Rinse and wipe it before the next glass.
flow.kid: Dip the probe. Wait for the number. Write it. Wipe the probe. Then do the next glass.
flow.parent: Typical readings: tap water reads many hundreds in some cities and far less in others. Purifier water usually reads far lower than tap water. Bottled water reads between the two. Salty water reads high. Sugary water reads close to the tap water reading. Your numbers will differ, so compare the glasses with each other. A TDS meter does not count the dissolved things directly. It measures how well the water carries electricity, which needs charged particles. Sugar is not charged, so the meter barely notices it. With the saucer test, the tap water leaves a visible white ring, the purifier water a fainter one, and the salty water a thick crust. Sugar leaves a sticky film. With 2 to 4 children, each tests one glass and shares the numbers. Do not drink the test glasses.
flow.context: In this step you measure all five glasses with the meter.

flow.do: Ask your child to compare the readings. Ask why the sugar water and the salt water gave such different readings.
flow.say: Look at the numbers. Which glass is highest? Which is lowest? Sugar and salt both dissolved. Why did they read so differently?
flow.kid: Compare the numbers. Why did sugar read so low and salt so high?

check.q: Sugar dissolved fully in the water, yet the TDS meter barely changed. What is the best explanation?
options: The meter measures charged particles, and sugar does not make any
Sugar did not really dissolve
The meter was broken
check.why: A TDS meter senses how well the water carries electricity, and that needs charged particles called ions. Salt makes ions, but sugar molecules stay whole and carry no charge. So the meter misses sugar even though it is dissolved.

flow.context: In this step you compare the readings and explain the sugar result.

projects.title: Kitchen Dyes: which colours stay in cloth?
projects.context: In this project you make dyes from kitchen things, dye white cloth, and wash it the next day to see which colours stay.

materials.item: four squares of white cotton cloth, 15 centimetres by 15 centimetres, cut from an old white handkerchief or sheet
a handful of dry onion skins
two teaspoons of turmeric powder
one small beetroot, grated
two tablespoons of tea leaves
four small steel pans or old vessels you do not mind staining, four small bowls for soaking, a strainer, a spoon and tongs
water, soap, a clothes line or string, and clips
scissors, to cut each cloth in half

projects.safety: A grown-up does all the simmering and handles the hot dye. Let the dye cool before the child touches it. Do not drink the dye. The dyes stain clothes and the sink, so wear old clothes.

schedule.what: Make four dyes, dye four cloths and hang them to dry overnight.
Cut each cloth in half, wash one half, dry it and compare with the unwashed half.

projects.record: Make a table with four rows: onion skin, turmeric, beetroot and tea. Write the colour and a darkness score from 0 to 5 before washing and after washing. Then glue or tape the two halves of each cloth beside the table.

setup.art: Four small steel pans on a stove, each with a different kitchen material in water: onion skin, turmeric, beetroot and tea.
setup.caption: 1. A grown-up simmers each material in water for ten minutes.

setup.art: A white cloth square being pushed under the coloured dye in a pan with a spoon.
setup.caption: 2. Soak a damp cloth in each cooled dye for half an hour.

setup.art: Four dyed cloth squares of different colours hanging on a string with clips.
setup.caption: 3. Hang them up to dry overnight.

setup.art: Each cloth cut in half, with one half washed in a basin and the other kept dry for comparison.
setup.caption: 4. Next day, wash half of each cloth. Compare.

flow.do: Show your child the four materials and the white cloth. Ask which dye they think will stay in the cloth best and which will wash out first.
flow.say: We will make four dyes. Then we will wash the cloth. Which dye do you think will stay the longest? Which will wash out first? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: There are four dyes. Which will stay in the cloth after washing? Which will wash out? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think that colour will stay best?
good: It is the strongest colour.
Onion skin is brown like old cloth.
Turmeric stains everything.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guesses. Turmeric stains fingers and plates, so many children guess it will hold best. Write the guesses.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Kitchen Dyes project. You guess before you dye.

flow.do: 1. A grown-up puts each material in its own pan with two cups of water. 2. Bring each to a gentle simmer for ten minutes. 3. Strain the dye into a cup or a bowl. 4. Let it cool until comfortable to touch.
flow.say: A grown-up will simmer each material in water for ten minutes. The hot water pulls the colour out of the material. Which colours dissolved into the water?
flow.kid: A grown-up simmers each material in water. The colour dissolves into the water. Let it cool.
flow.parent: Hot water dissolves colour faster, just as it dissolves sugar faster. Strain out the skins, tea leaves and beetroot, so you are left with coloured water. Label the four bowls. Old pans may stay stained. With 2 to 4 children, each child takes one dye and its cloth. One child alone can do two dyes (onion and turmeric) on day 1 if time is short. Keep children away from the stove.
flow.context: In this step a grown-up makes four dyes by simmering kitchen things in water.

flow.do: 1. Wet each white cloth under the tap and squeeze it. 2. Push one cloth into each cooled dye so it is fully covered. 3. Stir now and then for half an hour. For a stronger colour, leave it soaking for a few hours. 4. Take out each cloth. 5. Rinse it briefly in cold water until the water runs lighter. 6. Hang it up to dry overnight.
flow.say: Push each cloth into a dye. Move it around so the colour takes evenly. After half an hour, take it out, rinse it lightly and hang it up.
flow.kid: Soak a damp cloth in each dye for half an hour. Rinse lightly. Hang to dry.
flow.parent: The cloths look darker wet than dry. Tea and onion skin usually give tan or orange-brown. Turmeric gives a bright yellow. Beetroot gives a pink that may look weak, and sometimes only beige. Nothing is added to fix the dye to the cloth, so the colours are gentle, which is fine for the test. Use cotton, as nylon or polyester will not take the dye. Hang the cloths where drips do not matter.
flow.context: In this step you soak four cloths in four dyes and hang them to dry.

flow.do: 1. Next day, cut each dry cloth in half. 2. Keep one half dry. 3. Wash the other half in warm soapy water, rubbing it 20 times. 4. Rinse and hang to dry.
flow.say: Cut each cloth in half. Keep one half as it is. Wash the other half with soap and rub it twenty times. Which colours stay? Which fade?
flow.kid: Cut each cloth in half. Wash one half. Rub it twenty times. Rinse and dry it.
flow.parent: Washing is a fair test only if every cloth is rubbed the same number of times and rinsed the same way. Dry the washed halves quickly in a breeze or under a fan.
flow.context: On the second day you cut each cloth in half and wash one half.

flow.do: 1. Lay the washed half beside the unwashed half for each colour. 2. Give each half a darkness score from 0 to 5. 3. Write which faded the most and which faded the least. 4. Ask your child to say what they think, what they saw, and why.
flow.say: Put the washed half beside the dry half. Which colour is almost the same? Which is much paler? What do you think now? What did you see? Why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Put the washed half beside the dry half. Which faded most? Which faded least?
flow.parent: Results vary with cloth and water, so write exactly what you see. Turmeric often fades a lot in washing and in sun, beetroot usually fades to a weak pink or beige, and tea and onion skin usually hold best. A dye that washes out easily was only loosely held by the cloth, so the water could take it back.

check.q: A dyed cloth loses much of its colour when washed. What does this suggest about that dye?
options: The cloth held it loosely, so the water could take it back
The dye was not coloured enough
The soap made new colour
check.why: A dye that stays in cloth is held on by the cloth. A dye that washes out is only loosely held, so soap and water can dissolve it again. Soap does not make colour, and strong colour does not always mean strong hold.

flow.context: In this step you compare the washed and dry halves and say what you found.

challenges.title: Rescue the Salt: separate a four-part mix
challenges.context: This is a design challenge. A bowl holds a mix of four things. You plan the order of steps that gets every one back separately, including the salt.
challenges.problem: A bowl holds one tablespoon each of rice, rava and salt, and five steel paper clips, all mixed together. Plan and carry out a way to get all four back as separate piles, with the salt dry and clean. Use only things from home.
challenges.safety: A grown-up does any heating on the stove. Do not taste or eat any part of the mix.
constraints: Do not taste or eat any part of the mix.
A grown-up must do any heating on the stove.
Your plan must be written down before you start.
Every pile must be as pure as you can make it.
materials: a bowl with one tablespoon each of rice, rava and salt mixed with five steel paper clips
a fridge magnet or a small magnet
a steel tea strainer or a kitchen sieve
a glass of water, a spoon, and a thin cotton cloth
two clean bowls and a flat steel plate
a sunny window, or a grown-up with a stove and a small pan
general: Use the magnet to pick out the paper clips first, because only the steel is magnetic.
Pour the mix through the strainer. The rice stays in it, and the rava and salt fall through.
Stir the rava and salt into water. The salt dissolves and the rava does not. Pour it through the cloth to keep the rava.
Pour the salty water onto the plate and let the water evaporate in the sun, or heat it gently, until white salt is left.
creative: Wrap the magnet in a thin plastic bag, so the clips come off the bag easily when you take the magnet away.
Use warm water for the salt step, so the salt dissolves faster.
Put a damp cloth over a bowl and tip the rava and salt on it with water. The salt water drips through and the rava stays on the cloth.
Test your salt pile by dropping a little of it into clean water. It should dissolve and leave no bits. Do not taste it.
challenges.your_turn: Draw your plan as a chain of steps. Write the reason for each step. Try it, then write down which pile was hardest to get clean and why. Could you change the order of the steps? What would go wrong?

setup.art: A steel bowl holding a mix of rice, rava, white salt and steel paper clips.
setup.caption: 1. Look at the mix. Plan the order of your steps on paper.

setup.art: A magnet lifting paper clips from the mix, and a tea strainer holding rice above a bowl of rava and salt.
setup.caption: 2. Take out the clips with the magnet. Strain out the rice.

setup.art: Rava and salt stirred in a glass of water, then poured through a cloth into a bowl.
setup.caption: 3. Dissolve the salt in water. Pour it through a cloth to catch the rava.

setup.art: A steel plate of salty water in a sunny window, with white crystals forming at its edge.
setup.caption: 4. Let the salty water evaporate. The salt stays behind.

flow.do: 1. Read the problem together. 2. Ask your child to write the order of steps and the reason for each. 3. Check that the plan uses each difference: which thing is magnetic, which is the biggest, and which dissolves in water.
flow.say: Four things are mixed. Each has something different about it. Which one is magnetic? Which one is the biggest? Which one dissolves in water? Plan the order of your steps and say why.
flow.kid: Four things are mixed. Plan the order of steps. Say why for each step.

ask.q: Which step should come first, and why?
good: The magnet, because it only takes the clips and nothing else.
The strainer, because it is dry and quick.
Water should come last, because it makes everything wet.

flow.parent: A good plan does the dry steps first and the water step last. Once water is added, the rice and clips would be wet and harder to separate. Write the plan down.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Rescue the Salt challenge. You plan the steps.

flow.do: 1. Follow the plan to take out the clips and the rice. 2. Put each in its own pile. 3. Look at what is left in the bowl.
flow.say: Do the dry steps first. Take out the clips with the magnet. Strain out the rice. What is left in the bowl?
flow.kid: Use the magnet to take out the clips. Use the strainer to take out the rice. What is left?
flow.parent: If some rava stays on the rice, tap the strainer. Clips that stick to each other are fine. Check that no clips are left in the mix.
flow.context: In this step you take out the paper clips with the magnet and the rice with the strainer.

flow.do: 1. Put the rava and salt in a glass of water. 2. Stir for two minutes. 3. Lay the cloth over a clean bowl. 4. Pour the mix slowly through the cloth. 5. Rinse the rava on the cloth with a little water.
flow.say: Stir the rava and salt into water. Which one disappears? Pour it through the cloth. What stays on the cloth, and what goes through?
flow.kid: Stir rava and salt into water. Pour it through a cloth. What stays on the cloth?
flow.parent: The salt dissolves and goes through the cloth. The rava stays on the cloth. Wash the rava with a spoon of water so no salt stays in it.

check.q: Why does the salt go through the cloth, but the rava stays on it?
options: The salt has dissolved into pieces far smaller than the cloth's holes, and rava has not dissolved
Rava is heavier than salt
The cloth likes salt
check.why: Dissolved salt is in tiny pieces that pass through any cloth, but rava does not dissolve and stays as bits that are too big to pass. Weight does not matter here, and a cloth does not like anything.

flow.context: In this step you dissolve the salt in water and catch the rava with a cloth.

flow.wait: Leave the plate in a sunny window until dry
flow.do: 1. Pour the salty water onto the flat plate. 2. Put it in a sunny window. 3. A grown-up may heat it gently in a small pan instead, until a white crust forms. 4. Look at the plate later.
flow.say: Pour the salty water onto the plate. Where will the water go? What will be left? Wait until the water has gone, and look.
flow.kid: Pour the salty water on a plate. Put it in the sun. Look at it later.
flow.parent: In a sunny window the water may take several hours to dry, or a day in damp weather. With the stove, a grown-up heats it gently for about ten minutes, and stops as soon as white crystals show. Do not let it burn.
flow.context: In this step you let the water evaporate to get the dry salt back.

flow.do: Line up the four piles. Ask your child which was easiest to separate and which was hardest. Ask what would go wrong with a different order.
flow.say: Here are your four piles. Which was easiest? Which was hardest to get clean? What would have gone wrong if you had added water first?
flow.kid: Line up the four piles. Which was hardest? What if you added water first?
flow.parent: A strong answer says that each step used a different difference between the things: magnetism, size, dissolving in water, and evaporation. The water step must come after the dry steps, because it dissolves the salt and makes everything else wet.
flow.context: In this step you compare the four piles and think about the order of steps.

items.p: Which of these dissolves much better in oil than in water?
items.why: Turmeric colour is oily, so it dissolves in oil. Salt and sugar dissolve in water. Food colour for cakes is made to dissolve in water.

items.p: Sort these. Does each one dissolve mostly in water or mostly in oil?
items.a: see items
items.why: Charged and sticky things such as salt, sugar and honey dissolve in water. Oily things such as camphor, chilli heat and ghee dissolve in oil.

items.p: The liquid that does the dissolving in a solution is called the ____.
items.why: The solvent is the liquid that dissolves the other thing. The thing that dissolves is the solute.

items.p: Oil and water can never be made to mix, however you try.
items.why: False. A drop of soap lets oil spread through water as tiny drops, which is how milk and mayonnaise stay mixed. The oil is not dissolved, but it does stay mixed.

items.p: What does it mean to dilute a salty solution?
opts: Add more water, so the same salt is spread through more liquid
items.why: To dilute is to add more solvent. The amount of salt stays the same, but it is spread out, so each sip tastes less salty. Adding salt would make it stronger.

items.p: Match each word to what it means.
pairs: the liquid that does the dissolving
how much is dissolved in a certain amount of liquid
add more liquid so the solution is weaker
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: These four words describe every solution, whether it is salt in water or turmeric in oil.

items.p: A glass of liquid is cloudy, a torch beam shows up inside it, and nothing settles at the bottom after an hour. What is it most likely to be?
items.why: A solution is clear. A suspension settles. A cloudy liquid that shows the beam and does not settle is a colloid, like milk.

items.p: A grown-up bites a hot chilli. Why does a spoon of curd soothe the burn better than a sip of water?
items.a: The hot part of a chilli dissolves in fat and hardly in water. Curd has fat, so the hot chemical dissolves into it and is carried away. Water just spreads it around.
items.why: A strong answer says that the hot chemical is fat-soluble, and that curd has fat while water does not take it up.

items.p: A warm soda holds more gas than a cold soda.
items.why: False. Warm liquids hold less gas. That is why a warm soda foams and goes flat quickly, and a cold soda keeps its fizz.

items.p: A sealed bottle of soda shows no bubbles at all, yet it is full of gas. Where is the gas?
opts: Dissolved in the liquid, squeezed in by pressure
There is no gas until you open it
items.why: In the sealed bottle the pressure squeezes the gas into the water, where it spreads out as tiny pieces. When you open the bottle the pressure drops and the gas comes out as bubbles.

items.p: Put the steps of the Kulfi in a Bag test in order.
items: Shake both bags for ten minutes
Put ice in both bags and salt in only one
Compare the milk in the two small bags
Seal sweet milk in two small bags
a: Seal sweet milk in two small bags
Put ice in both bags and salt in only one
Shake both bags for ten minutes
Compare the milk in the two small bags
items.why: First set up both bags the same way. Then change only the salt. Then shake for the same time. Last, compare the results.

items.p: Which one is not a solution?
items.why: Milk is a colloid. It has tiny fat drops floating in it, and a torch beam shows up in it. The other three are solutions.

items.p: Draw two glasses of soda just after they are opened. Show a cold soda and a warm soda. Draw the bubbles in each.
items.a: The cold soda with a gentle thread of small bubbles. The warm soda with many large bubbles and foam rising over the top.
items.why: A good drawing shows that the warm soda lets out gas much faster than the cold soda.
items.art: Two empty tall glass outlines side by side.

items.p: Label the drawing of a soap molecule at the edge of a grease drop in water: the head, the tail, the water, the grease.
items.a: The head faces the water. The tail points into the grease. The water is outside the drop. The grease is the drop.
items.why: A soap molecule has a water-loving head and an oil-loving tail. The tail sticks into the grease and the head stays in the water.
items.art: A round grease drop in water with one tadpole-shaped soap molecule on the drop edge, and four blank label lines.

items.p: A plastic tiffin box has a yellow turmeric stain that plain water does not remove. What would you try, and why?
items.a: Rub a little oil on the stain first, then wash with soap. Turmeric colour dissolves in oil, so the oil takes it up, and soap washes the oil away.
items.why: A strong answer uses the idea that turmeric colour dissolves in oil, and says that soap is needed to rinse the oil away.

items.p: A girl has a yellow turmeric stain on her white plastic box. Three people in her family suggest ways to clean it.

views.says: Wash it with hot water and soap.
Rub a little coconut oil on it first, then wash.
Scrub it hard with plain cold water.

items.ask: Whose way would you try first? Give a reason from what you know about turmeric. Then say one good point about another way.
items.a: A strong answer picks the grandmother's way, because turmeric colour dissolves in oil, so oil lifts it. A fair point about the mother's way is that soap and hot water do help rinse away the oil and dissolve the colour a little. The brother's way is the least likely to work, because cold water cannot take the colour.
items.why: Several ways can work, but the best one matches the science: the colour is fat-soluble. A good answer weighs the others fairly.

items.p: Why does a mix of ice and salt get colder than plain ice?
opts: The salt dissolves in the thin film of water on the ice and lowers its freezing point, so the melting ice takes more heat from the mixture
Salt is stored in a cold place
items.why: Dissolved salt makes it harder for water to freeze, so the ice keeps melting below zero degrees. Melting takes heat, so the mixture gets colder. Salt itself is not cold.

items.p: On a hot afternoon, fish in a small still pond swim to the top and open their mouths. Use what you know about gases to explain why.
items.a: Fish take in oxygen that is dissolved in the water. Warm water holds less dissolved gas than cool water, so there is less oxygen for the fish. They come to the surface where the water meets the air.
items.why: A strong answer says that oxygen dissolves in water, that warm water holds less, and that the surface gets more oxygen from the air.

items.p: A TDS meter reads about 20 in a glass of water with a teaspoon of sugar stirred in, and about 20 in plain filtered water. What is the best explanation?
opts: The meter reads charged particles, and sugar makes none
Sugar water is the same as salt water
items.why: A TDS meter senses electricity carried by charged particles. Sugar dissolves into whole molecules with no charge, so the meter does not notice it. Sugar did dissolve, and it is very different from salt.

items.p: Sea water holds about 35 grams of salt in every litre. About how many grams of salt are in 2 litres?
items.why: Each litre holds 35 grams. 2 litres hold 35 + 35, which is 70 grams.

items.p: Almost nothing is completely insoluble in water. Even rock dissolves a very little.
items.why: True. Rainwater slowly dissolves limestone and carves caves. A thing we call insoluble just dissolves too little for us to see in a short time.

items.p: Why does soap lift grease off a plate?
opts: Its tail grips the grease and its head grips the water, so the grease is carried off in tiny drops
items.why: A soap molecule has an oil-loving tail and a water-loving head. The grease is broken into tiny drops wrapped in soap, and water carries them away. The grease is not truly dissolved.

items.p: Sort these vitamins. Does each one dissolve in fat or in water?
items.a: see items
items.why: Vitamins A, D, E and K dissolve in fat. Vitamins B and C dissolve in water. So a little oil in a meal helps the body take in vitamins A, D, E and K.

items.p: Put these in order, from the lowest freezing point to the highest.
items.why: The more salt dissolved, the lower the freezing point. Very salty brine freezes at about minus 20 degrees, sea water at about minus 2, and pure water at zero.

items.p: A friend says milk is a solution because it looks the same all through. How could you show that milk is not a solution?
items.a: Shine a torch through the side of a glass of milk in water. A solution would hardly show the beam, but milk shows a bright beam because tiny drops of fat float in it and scatter the light.
items.why: A strong answer names the torch test and says what it shows: floating bits that are too small to see.

items.p: Label the drawing of a cell skin: the water outside, the water inside, the heads, the tails.
items.a: Water on the outside and water on the inside. Two rows of heads facing the water on each side. The tails together in the middle.
items.why: The skin is a double layer. The water-loving heads face the water on both sides and the oil-loving tails hide in the middle.
items.art: A double row of tadpole-shaped molecules between two blue areas, with four blank label lines.

items.p: Which one is not an emulsion?
items.why: An emulsion is tiny drops of one liquid spread through another liquid. Salt water is a solution, with nothing floating in it.

items.p: Plan a fair test to find out whether sugar dissolves in oil. Say what you will keep the same and what you will change.
items.a: Put the same amount of sugar in the same amount of water and in the same amount of oil, in matching jars, and stir the same way for the same time. Only the liquid changes. Look at the bottom and at how clear each liquid is.
items.why: A strong plan changes only the liquid and keeps the amount of sugar, the amount of liquid, the jar, the stirring and the time the same.

items.p: Draw a drop of food colour falling into a still glass of water. Draw it at the start, after one minute, and after ten minutes.
items.a: A dark drop at the top at the start, a spreading cloud of colour after one minute, and an even pale colour through the whole glass after ten minutes.
items.why: A good drawing shows the colour spreading out until it is even, without anyone stirring, because the dissolved particles keep moving.
items.art: Three empty glass outlines in a row labelled start, one minute and ten minutes.

items.p: Rainwater slowly dissolves limestone and makes caves. Why does it take so long?
opts: Limestone dissolves only a very little each time, so it takes a very long time to remove a lot
items.why: Limestone dissolves very slowly. Each drop of rainwater takes away only a tiny amount, but over hundreds of thousands of years the amount adds up to a cave.

items.p: Something that does not dissolve in water cannot dissolve in oil either.
items.why: False. Turmeric colour, chilli heat and camphor hardly dissolve in water, but they dissolve in oil. Each liquid takes different things.

items.p: A water molecule has slightly charged ____, which let it hold on to salt.
items.why: One end of a water molecule is slightly negative and the other end is slightly positive. These ends grip the charged particles in salt.

items.p: Which soda will lose its fizz fastest after being opened?
opts: A warm soda that is stirred
A cold soda in a closed bottle
items.why: Warmth makes the water hold less gas, and stirring gives the gas many places to escape. A cold soda left still loses gas slowly, and a closed bottle keeps the pressure in.

items.p: Plan a test to find out whether warmth changes how much gas a soda gives off. Name what you will keep the same, what you will change, and how you will measure the gas.
items.a: Use two bottles of the same soda, one cold and one warm. Open both the same way, put a balloon of the same kind on each, swirl them the same, and measure the balloons after the same time. Only the warmth changes. The size of the balloon shows how much gas came out.
items.why: A strong plan keeps the drink, bottle, balloon, opening and swirling the same, changes only the warmth and measures the gas with the balloon.

items.p: William Henry found that the mass of gas that dissolves in a liquid is in proportion to the pressure. If the pressure on a sealed soda is doubled, about how much more gas will dissolve?
items.why: In proportion means that doubling the pressure doubles the gas that dissolves. That is why a sealed bottle holds so much more gas than an open glass.

items.p: A salt pan dries up 200 litres of sea water that held 35 grams of salt in every litre. How many grams of salt are left behind?
items.why: Each litre leaves 35 grams. 200 times 35 is 7000 grams, which is 7 kilograms.

items.p: On a mountain road in the Himalayas, ice forms on the road in winter. Three people say what to do.

views.says: Spread salt on the road. It melts the ice, so vehicles can pass safely.
Salt washes into streams and soil and harms the plants and animals there. Use less.
Spread sand instead. It does not melt the ice, but it gives the tyres grip.

items.ask: Which would you choose? Give a reason from what you know about salt and ice. Then say one good point about another idea.
items.a: A strong answer says that salt lowers the freezing point so ice melts, but it only works down to about minus 10 or minus 20 degrees, and in colder weather it cannot help. It weighs this against the harm to streams. Sand gives grip without chemicals. A fair answer picks one idea, gives a reason, and says one good point about another idea.
items.why: Each idea has a cost. Salt melts ice but stops working in deep cold and can harm nature. Sand gives grip but does not remove the ice.

items.p: Why do kulfi sellers pack ice and salt around the kulfi pot?
opts: Salty ice is colder than plain ice, so it can freeze the kulfi
Salt makes the ice last longer
items.why: Plain ice cannot freeze sweet milk, because melting ice stays at zero degrees. Salty ice can fall to about minus 20 degrees, which freezes the kulfi.

items.p: Explain why oil does not dissolve in water. Use the idea of the water molecule's slightly charged ends.
items.a: Water molecules have slightly charged ends, which let them hold on to each other and to charged or sticky things. Oil molecules have no such ends, so water holds on to other water instead and pushes the oil out. The oil joins into drops and floats.
items.why: A strong answer says water holds on to its own kind and to charged or sticky things, and has nothing to grip on oil.

items.p: Match each thing to what it does.
pairs: has a water-loving head and an oil-loving tail
senses charged particles dissolved in water
is a double layer of molecules with tails hiding from water
is dissolved under pressure and escapes when the bottle opens
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Each one shows how a dissolved thing or a molecule behaves in water.

items.p: Sea water freezes at a slightly lower temperature than fresh water.
items.why: True. Dissolved salt lowers the freezing point, so sea water freezes at about minus 2 degrees Celsius instead of zero.

items.p: Which one is not an example of a dissolved gas leaving a liquid?
opts: Bubbles rising from a poured soda
Fish gasping in a warm pond
Big steam bubbles rising in a rolling boil
Tiny bubbles forming on the side of a warming pan of water
items.why: The big bubbles at a rolling boil are water vapour, water that has turned into a gas. The other three are about gases that were dissolved in the liquid and come out as it warms or the pressure falls.

items.p: The word insoluble really means 'dissolves too little for us to notice'. Explain what this means for a piece of limestone in rain.
items.a: Each raindrop dissolves only a tiny bit of the limestone. In one day we cannot see any change. But over hundreds of thousands of years the water can dissolve enough to carve a cave. So insoluble depends on how little dissolves and how long we wait.
items.why: A strong answer says that a very small amount dissolving, over a very long time, adds up to a lot.

items.p: Draw a zoomed-in picture of a soap molecule at the edge of a grease drop in water.
items.a: A grease drop in the middle, with tadpole-shaped soap molecules around the drop, tails pointing into the grease and heads pointing out into the water.
items.why: The tail grips the grease and the head grips the water, so the soap wraps the grease in a ring.
items.art: A large empty circle labelled 'zoomed in'.

items.p: Sort these mixtures into the three kinds.
items.a: see items
items.why: A solution is clear and never settles. A suspension settles. A colloid has tiny bits that never settle and scatter light, like milk and fog.

items.p: A bottle of soda is opened, closed again, and left in a cold fridge for a day. It is now almost flat even though it is cold. Why?
opts: When it was opened the pressure fell and much of the gas escaped, and the closed bottle could not squeeze it back
items.why: Opening the bottle let the pressure drop, so most of the dissolved gas left as bubbles. Closing it again does not push the gas back into the water. Cold water holds gas well, but there was little gas left.

items.p: Label the Kulfi in a Bag set-up: the small bag of milk, the big bag, the ice, the salt and the towel.
items.a: The small bag of milk in the middle. The big bag around it. The ice packed around the small bag. The salt sprinkled in the ice. The towel wrapped around the outside.
items.why: The milk sits in the coldest part, surrounded by salty ice, and the towel protects the hands.
items.art: A big zip bag wrapped in a towel with a small bag inside, ice around it, and five blank label lines.

items.p: Put the steps of the Rescue the Salt challenge in the best order.
items: Dissolve the salt in water and pour through a cloth
Take out the clips with a magnet
a: Take out the clips with a magnet
Dissolve the salt in water and pour through a cloth
items.why: Do the dry steps first, because they use magnetism and size. Water comes later because it dissolves the salt and wets the rest. Evaporation comes last to get the salt back.

items.p: A child gets these results: the balloon on a cold soda measured 14 centimetres around, and the balloon on a warm soda measured 28 centimetres around. Write a claim, the evidence and the reasoning.
items.a: Claim: a warm soda lets out more gas than a cold soda. Evidence: the warm soda's balloon went to 28 centimetres and the cold soda's to 14, twice as far around. Reasoning: gas is dissolved in the drink, and warm liquid holds less of it, so more escapes into the balloon.
items.why: A strong answer states the claim, uses the two numbers as evidence and explains why warmth makes gas leave.

quiz.p: Which of these dissolves in oil but hardly in water?
quiz.why: The orange colour of carrots is carotene, which dissolves in fat. Sugar, salt and lemon juice all dissolve in water.

quiz.p: A turmeric stain on a plastic box does not come off with plain water. What is likely to lift it?
quiz.why: Turmeric colour dissolves in oil, so oil takes it up and soap rinses the oil away. Cold water and salt water cannot take the colour.

quiz.p: After eating a hot chilli, which helps most?
opts: A spoon of curd, because the hot chemical dissolves in fat
A big glass of water, because water washes it away
quiz.why: The hot chemical in chilli dissolves in fat and hardly in water. Curd has fat, so it takes the chemical up. Water only spreads it around.

quiz.p: Why does a warm soda go flat faster than a cold soda?
opts: Warm water holds less dissolved gas
The bubbles in warm soda are bigger
quiz.why: The warmer the water, the less gas it can hold, so the gas leaves sooner. The size of the bubbles is not the reason.

quiz.p: A sealed bottle of soda has no bubbles. What keeps the gas dissolved?
opts: The high pressure inside the bottle
quiz.why: High pressure squeezes the gas into the water. When the pressure drops at opening, the gas comes out as bubbles.

quiz.p: You shine a torch through a glass of liquid from the side and see a bright beam inside. After an hour nothing has settled. What kind of mixture is it?
quiz.why: A beam shows when floating bits scatter light, so it is not a solution. Nothing settled, so it is not a suspension. It is a colloid.

quiz.p: Salt is sprinkled on ice. What happens to the temperature of the mixture?
quiz.why: Dissolved salt lowers the freezing point, so the ice keeps melting below zero degrees, and melting takes heat from the mixture. It gets colder.

quiz.p: Why does salt help to freeze kulfi?
opts: Salty ice is colder than plain ice
quiz.why: Plain melting ice stays at zero, which is not cold enough. Salty ice falls much lower, enough to freeze sweet milk.

quiz.p: Why are caves found in limestone hills?
opts: Rainwater slowly dissolves the limestone over a very long time
The rock melts in the Sun
quiz.why: Rainwater carries a little carbon dioxide and slowly dissolves limestone. Over hundreds of thousands of years the rock is carved into caves.

quiz.p: What does the word insoluble really mean, if almost nothing is completely insoluble?
opts: It dissolves so little that we do not notice
quiz.why: Everything dissolves a very little. Insoluble means that so little dissolves that we cannot see it in a short time.

quiz.p: People once thought air was a single thing. What did Joseph Black find when he heated chalky stones?
opts: They gave off a gas that was not ordinary air
They became lighter because they dried
quiz.why: The stones lost weight because a gas escaped. This gas was different from ordinary air. It is carbon dioxide, which Priestley later dissolved in water.

quiz.p: Fish in a warm, still pond swim to the surface. What is the best explanation?
opts: Warm water holds less dissolved oxygen
quiz.why: Oxygen dissolves in water, and warm water holds less of it. At the surface, the water gets more oxygen from the air.

opts: Salt dissolves in water, and camphor dissolves in oil
Sugar dissolves in oil, and ghee dissolves in water
Salt dissolves in oil, and wax dissolves in water
quiz.why: Charged and sticky things such as salt dissolve in water. Oily things such as camphor dissolve in oil. The other pairs are the wrong way round.

applications: Fizzy drinks and goli soda hold carbon dioxide dissolved in cold water under pressure.
Soap, shampoo and washing powder lift oil and grease because one end of their molecules grips water and the other grips oil.
Cooks fry turmeric, chilli and other spices in oil at the start of a tadka, because their colours and flavours dissolve in oil.
Curd, buttermilk and raita soothe a hot chilli, because the hot chemical dissolves in their fat.
Kulfi and ice-cream makers pack ice with salt to make a mixture colder than ice alone.
In cold hill regions, salt is spread on icy roads to lower the freezing point of water.
Natural dyers extract colour from onion skins, turmeric and indigo with hot water, and fix it on cloth.
Doctors and pharmacists choose whether a medicine or vitamin must be taken with food, because some dissolve in fat and some in water.
Divers rise slowly from deep water, because gas dissolved in their blood under pressure can form bubbles if the pressure falls too fast.
Perfume makers in Kannauj make attars by catching the smell of flowers in sandalwood oil.
Fish keepers and pond managers watch the warmth of the water, because warm water holds less dissolved oxygen.
Water purifiers use TDS meters to estimate how much charged material is dissolved in the water.

open_questions.q: Why do bubbles begin at some places in a soda and not at others?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists know that bubbles start at tiny scratches and specks. They are still working out exactly how the very first tiny bubble forms inside a clear liquid.

open_questions.q: How much more carbon dioxide can the sea keep taking in as it grows warmer?
open_questions.why_open: Warm water holds less gas. The sea has taken in a large share of the carbon dioxide people release, but how long it can keep doing so is still being measured.

open_questions.q: How did the first cell skins form on the early Earth?
open_questions.why_open: Fat-like molecules form skins in water by themselves, which makes this seem possible. Nobody knows exactly how the first living cells came to have a skin.

open_questions.q: Why do chilli plants make a chemical that burns mammals, while birds eat them without a burn?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists have shown that birds eat chillies and spread their seeds, while mammals chew the seeds and destroy them. They think this is why the burn evolved, but they are still testing the idea.

open_questions.q: Can we design a drug that dissolves well in both water and fat?
open_questions.why_open: Many medicines must dissolve in the watery blood and also cross the fatty skin of a cell. Finding the balance for each new drug is one of the hard problems of medicine.

open_questions.q: Will sea water in the future dissolve rock and shell faster, as it takes in more carbon dioxide?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists see that the sea is slowly becoming a little more acidic, but how this will change shells, corals and reefs in each place is still being studied.
